articles.title: Monuments of India, Part 3: Sixteen Statues Sculpted from Photographs, a Rebuilt Mysore Palace and More
articles.description: Sixteen statues sculpted from photographs, finer animals, ships and traffic, about thirty new architectural parts, a rebuilt Mysore Palace and an 800k triangle budget for 101 Indian monuments built in three.js.
articles.body_html:
In Part 2 I went through the shared kit that every building in Monuments of India is made from: domes, kiosks, pillars, arches, temple towers. That kit made the famous buildings look much better. It also showed what was still crude. The statues were smooth figures without faces you could read, and several were stand-ins: a generic "leader" figure for Netaji, a seated Buddha for Adi Shankaracharya, Hindu deities on the roofs of Kolkata's Victoria Memorial. The Nandis, elephants and lions guarding the temples were simple shapes. The boats and traffic were boxes. And several monuments still looked like massing models, with the right shape and height but plain walls and empty courts.

This post covers the round of work that went after all of that:

  1. Statues: every free-standing statue sculpted again from photographs, sixteen in all, from the Statue of Unity to the lion and tiger on the gates of Mumbai's Victoria Terminus.
  2. Animals and figures: Nandi, temple elephants, lions, war horses, door guardians and frieze figures.
  3. Boats, ships, traffic and guns: cargo ships, Kashmiri houseboats, the traffic on Kolkata's and Mumbai's bridges, and the Kargil memorial's guns.
  4. Architecture: about thirty new shared parts and new surfaces, finer detail on more than forty monuments, and Mysore Palace rebuilt from a photograph.
  5. A bigger triangle budget: 800k on desktops instead of 650k, spent on the buildings and not the trees.

Most pictures below are before-and-after pairs, rendered by the project's own screenshot scripts.

Statues

The statues are not built from boxes and cylinders. Each one is a signed distance field, a function that tells you how far any point is from the figure's skin, turned into a mesh. Until now each statue was meshed on one grid. That meant a choice: a fine grid everywhere was too many triangles, and a coarse one gave the head no face.

The sculpting function now takes a list of fine regions. The part of the figure inside a region, usually an ellipsoid round the head, is meshed on its own finer grid, and the rest on the main grid. The two parts overlap slightly at the seam, and each is drawn just inside the skin past its cut, so they meet in one clean line. This is how Nandi's head gets 3.5 cm cells while its body has 8 cm:

sculpt('nandi', nandiField, {
  h: 0.08,            // body: 8 cm cells
  wear: 0.4,          // ridges rubbed pale, as polished stone is
  split: {            // head: its own finer grid
    region: E([0, 2.38, 2.25], [0.9, 1.15, 0.78]), // ellipsoid crossing the neck
    h: 0.035,
    lo: [-1.0, 1.1, 1.4], hi: [1.0, 3.5, 3.05],
  },
});

Two more tools came with it: wear, which rubs the ridges pale (worked out from the field's curvature), and snap(), a way to lay curves and parts on the skin, such as buttons, creepers, hems and jewellery, so they follow the surface instead of floating beside it.

The biggest change in how the statues are made is that hands, faces and feet are no longer separate meshes stuck onto a body. They are sculpted in the body, as one skin, with fine regions that follow them. The Statue of Unity was done this way first, and then every other statue was brought up to the same standard and checked against photographs.

Here is every statue in the project now. The components page has the same gallery with a table of what each one is and where it's built:
Sardar Patel, Statue of Unity Bahubali, Gommateshwara Thiruvalluvar, Kanyakumari
The seated Shiva, Nageshwar Adi Shankaracharya, Kedarnath Statue of Oneness, Omkareshwar
Netaji, India Gate Shivaji, Gateway of India Angel of Victory and Queen Victoria
Justice, Prudence, Motherhood, Learning, Britannia Progress, Victoria Terminus Commerce and Agriculture, Victoria Terminus
Gajalakshmi, Mysore Palace The Lion Capital; the lion and tiger of Victoria Terminus

The four great statues

The Statue of Unity was redone from photographs, layer by layer, then checked against them again:

  • The head: the face from the 1949 portrait, a little smaller and bowed, with a heavy brow, deep-set open eyes under heavy lids, forehead lines, a strong nose, deep folds to a set mouth, jowls and ears.
  • The upper body in three layers: a short square shawl to the elbows with a turned-up hem and creases over the arms. Under it is the bandi, a sleeveless jacket with a band collar, eight buttons, a chest pocket and two flapped pockets, with a wide opening that the viewing gallery's windows sit across. Below that is an A-line kurta. The kurta sleeves and the loose fists are sculpted in the body; the separate mesh hands are gone.
  • The dhoti: full, in long diagonal folds round each leg and hanging in swags between them, narrowing to an uneven hem above the ankle.
  • The feet: bare shins and chappals with a shaped sole, a strap over the instep and a toe ring, and five toes. Before, they were boot-like lumps on flat discs.
  • The bronze: a new plates surface draws the cladding as joined bronze panels, with joints worked out in 3D space so they run true over the curved body. The colour is now the dull olive-gold of the real statue, and the plate joints are softened.

The plinth also gained the museum's glazed entrance at the top of the front steps, and stone fins between the bronze panels of the top tier.

Before After

Gommateshwara, the monolith at Shravanabelagola, now stands at its real 17.4 m:

  • The head is meshed at 4.5 cm: almond eyes under lowered lids, arched brows, a straight nose, a smiling mouth, long flat earlobes, and small curls in rows on the scalp.
  • The legs are carved as massive columns, the thighs meeting from the groin to the knees, on large feet with toes. The shoulders slope as they do in the stone.
  • The hands have a flat palm, four long separate fingers and a thumb, meshed on fine cells, resting on two taller anthills that are one stone with the legs and carved with spiral scrolls.
  • The madhavi creepers rise from between the feet, sweep out across the thighs in a V and wind up the arms to a coil below the shoulder, in granite, in low relief on the skin. Before, they floated in green beside the limbs.
Before After

Thiruvalluvar at Kanyakumari is 29 m tall on the Alankara Mandapam, now a pilastered granite hall with a terrace and parapet. The face, beard, moustache, hair knot and hands are sculpted in the body. He's turned so the right hand is raised before the chest and the left holds a bound palm-leaf manuscript at the waist, with the hips swaying and the feet under the hem. The real statue is built of stacked granite blocks, so a new blocks surface draws the joints between them.

The Shiva at Nageshwar was blue on a pink lotus. It's now as photographed: terracotta in colour, sitting in the half lotus with the left foot tucked under the right knee and the right foot lying sole up on the thigh, with toes and anklets. Four arms hold the trishul and a large damru, with Om on the raised palm. The face and hands are sculpted in the body, with painted eyes under lowered lids, a painted band of ash and the third eye. There are two malas in a V, a cobra with its hood upright beside the ear, snake armlets, tiger skins falling over the lap and shoulder, and the hair combed up into a knot with a pale crescent, on a rock seat with a tiger head.

Before After

Statues that were stand-ins

Several monuments had a statue in the right place but the wrong figure in it, borrowed from the kit. These were all sculpted from photographs.

  • Netaji at India Gate was the kit's generic "leader". He's now 8.5 m of black granite as one skin: saluting in INA uniform, the right hand flat at the edge of the side cap and the left fist at his side, round spectacles, a tunic with collar, shoulder straps, four flapped pockets and belt, breeches flaring over the thighs, and knee boots, with the uncut stone left behind the calves. The saluting hand uses a new slab() shape in the SDF library.
  • Shivaji at the Gateway of India was a cylinder-and-ball rider on one of Konark's horses. Now the bronze horse prances with its left foreleg raised (a new prance option on the horse), and the rider sits upright in angarkha, sash and baldric, a round shield on his back, the reins in his left hand and a curved sword held low along the flank, under a Maratha turban with plume and tassel. The tapering stone pedestal carries the shield and crossed swords and stands in a railed lawn.
  • The Statue of Oneness at Omkareshwar shows the young Shankaracharya walking, the staff across his body with a cloth bundle at its top, a water pot in his left hand, a long mala and rudraksha bands, in copper-toned bronze on an open lotus. It's meshed coarsely enough to keep the monument within its phone budget.
  • Adi Shankaracharya at Kedarnath was the kit's seated Buddha. He's now black stone, seated cross-legged (a new crossLegged() figure), with long hair, three rudraksha malas, the right hand raised in the gesture of teaching holding the flagged staff and the left on the knee with a palm-leaf book, on a great lotus bud on a post in a pool.
Before: the kit's generic figure After: Netaji, sculpted from photographs

Allegories for the colonial buildings

The Victoria Memorial and Victoria Terminus (CSMT) were using Hindu deity figures, the Buddha and Khajuraho poses on their roofs, because those were what the kit had. Their real statues are classical allegories, so there's now a kit for those: women in classical drapery sculpted as one skin, standing, seated (on a block or a throne, with a mantle, a child or an infant) or winged, with named arm poses and a head in hair, a veil and crown, or a helmet. And there's a set of things for them to hold: torch, sword, scales, mirror, book, palette, square, trident, caduceus, ship, plough, cornucopia, sheaf, sickle, wreath, trumpet, sceptre, orb, shield, winged wheel and star.

  • Victoria Memorial: the bronze Angel of Victory on top, winged and poised on her ball with a bugle to her lips and a wreath; Queen Victoria enthroned in the robes of the Star of India with crown, veil, sceptre and orb; Art, Architecture, Justice and Charity round the dome; Motherhood with Prudence and Learning over the north porch; and robed figures on the pavilion corners and the balustrade.
  • CSMT: Progress in marble on the dome, torch aloft and her hand on a winged wheel; the groups of Commerce and Agriculture over the forward wings' gables; robed figures by the clock; and the lion and tiger lying on the gate piers.

On phones the allegories become a light robed pose, which keeps both buildings within budget.

Animals and figures

The same sculpting tools went into the animals and figures that appear across dozens of monuments, so one improvement shows up everywhere they're used.

Nandi now has its head meshed at 3.5 cm, nostrils, mouth and lids, a saddle blanket with a raised border draped over its back, a strand of beads over the garland of bells, a larger bell at the chest, anklets and a tail tuft.

Before After

Elephants have a wrinkled trunk, rimmed ears, lidded eyes, a mouth and toenails. The dressed temple elephants are the bigger change. Their cloth, its gold border, the painted forehead and the nettipattam (the gold caparison on Kerala's temple elephants) used to be flat boxes and tilted plates. Now they're cast as thin shells on the skin, studded with bosses, with the bell rope laid round the neck. Elephants can also raise their trunks now, which is how the two beside Gajalakshmi at Mysore Palace pour water from their pots.

Before After

Lions are carved as temple gates carve them: a mane of curls in rows, a heavy brow over bulging eyes, the mouth open on fangs and a tongue, claws on the forepaws, a collar with a bell, and the tail curled up over the haunch to a flame-like tuft. The same lion now makes the Lion Capital on the National War Memorial, four lions back to back over the lotus bell (it used to be boxes and balls), and a lying-down couchant() pose for the lion and tiger at CSMT.

Horses follow Konark's war horses: muscled shoulders and quarters, proper knees, hocks and hooves, the mane carved in strands, and a full tail. They also have a bridle with cheek straps and noseband, a plume between the ears, bells on the breast collar and a saddle cloth.

Before After

Door guardians (dvarapalas) now have fierce faces, earrings, a tiered crown, necklace, armlets, belt and sash, and a ribbed club. Frieze figures, the rows of small carved people on temple walls, have a face with brow, nose and chin, and a tiered crown instead of a cone.

All this detail is tiered by size and device. A large lion on a desktop gets its head and mane meshed at 3 cm, while a small one in a frieze, or any lion on a phone, gets a coarser version.

Ships, boats, traffic and guns

The setting around each monument matters as much as the monument, and some of the props were still boxes.

Cargo ships in the harbours (off the Gateway of India, for example) are now proper general cargo ships about 90 m long. Each has a dark hull with red boot-topping and a white sheer line, hatch covers on the well deck, king posts with derricks, and a white superstructure in four tiers with a banded funnel. On desktops they also get window rows, bridge wings, lifeboats in davits, railings, anchors, a foremast and a radar mast.

Before After

Kashmiri houseboats have a long cedar hull with the bow raked up out of the water, a carved walnut-dark cabin under a gabled roof, and an open verandah at the bow with a carved railing and a fretted valance. On desktops they also get window frames and mullions, balusters, a ridge rail and a name board.

Before After

Traffic on the Howrah Bridge and the Bandra–Worli Sea Link is drawn from side profiles: saloons, Kolkata's yellow Ambassador taxis with their rounded bonnet and tall glasshouse, buses with a band of windows, and trucks with a painted wooden body under a tarpaulin. On desktops they also have lights, bumpers and destination boards, and phones get every other vehicle.

Before After

The Kargil War Memorial now shows the guns of the war on its plaza. There are three towed 155 mm howitzers modelled on the Bofors guns, each with its barrel and muzzle brake, recoil cylinders, shield, two big wheels and a split trail. In front is a row of plinths with the captured weapons: mortars, twin anti-aircraft guns and heavy machine guns on tripods.

Before After

Architecture

New parts in the kit

Most of the architectural gains come from new shared parts. Each is written once and then used wherever it belongs:
Manastambha Deepmala (lamp tower) Nandi mandapa
Iwan with muqarnas and an inscription band Pranala (water spout) Prayer wheels
Machicolation Copper and gilded-copper roofs Chadar (water cascade)

Temples

  • Manastambha: the pillar of honour in front of a Jain temple, optionally with four seated tirthankaras in its top pavilion.
  • Deepmala: Maharashtra's stone lamp tower, with rings of arms each carrying a brass lamp that lights at night.
  • Nandi mandapa: the open pavilion on the temple's axis where Nandi faces the sanctum.
  • Kerala gable: the carved timber mukhappu set into Kerala's temple roofs.
  • Dravida hall dress: a moulded base, pilasters, a curved kapota eave and a parapet of miniature shrines, for any plain South Indian hall or shrine block.
  • Carved door jambs (shakhas): columns of small figures in niches up the doorway, with Ganga and Yamuna at the foot.
  • Pranala: the spout draining the sanctum, a channelled trough ending in a makara head over a stone basin.
Before After

Mughal and Deccan

  • Muqarnas: tiers of small faceted cells lining the half-dome of the great arched recesses (iwans).
  • Inscription bands: black lettering inlaid in white marble round the frames.
  • Inlaid borders of white marble with small lozenges, glazed tile bands at Sher Shah's tomb and the Qutb Shahi tombs, and the petal ring round the Gol Gumbaz.
  • Bangla roofs, curved both ways, with the ridge and eaves drooping to the corners, as on Agra Fort's gilded pavilions and the Red Fort's jharokha.
  • Chadar: the Mughal garden cascade, a sloping marble bed carved in fish scales under a thin sheet of water.
Before After

Forts

  • Machicolations: boxes projecting from the head of a wall, with a slot in the floor for dropping stones on attackers.
  • Gun-loops in the merlons.
  • String courses and arrow slits on Mehrangarh's walls, and two rings of slits round each of Jaisalmer's 99 bastions.

Tibetan monasteries

  • Penbey parapets: the maroon band of packed twigs under the roof.
  • Framed hall windows with awnings, projecting timber window bays, galleries of brass prayer wheels, and gilded roofs with lotus-and-vase finials, upturned corners and bells.

Colonial

  • Louvred shutters at Cooch Behar Palace, and glazing behind the sun-breakers of Chandigarh's Capitol.

New surfaces

Some detail is too fine for geometry, so it's drawn by the surface shader instead:

  • Copper and gilded copper: staggered sheets with standing seams and hammer dimples, and verdigris along the seams on plain copper. Used on gilt roofs such as Kashi Vishwanath's and Tirumala's.
  • Terracotta: thin fired bricks, each its own shade with the odd one over-burnt, stained by soot and lichen. It fades to an even tone in the distance so it never shimmers. Used on Nalanda, the Dhamek Stupa, Ramappa's tower and the Cellular Jail.
  • Terracotta plaques: bands of moulded tiles with a lotus or a standing figure in turn.
  • Marble cladding that follows a curved shell, for the Lotus Temple's petals.
  • Granite blocks with their joints showing, for Thiruvalluvar.

Mysore Palace, rebuilt from a photograph

Mysore Palace got the biggest single change. It was a compact block with its tower standing out in front. It's now built to the proportions of the photographed front, about 125 m across and 44 m to the spire:

  • A ground floor with a row of small arches, and above it the Durbar Hall's arcade of wide cusped arches on paired granite columns over a pierced railing.
  • A gallery of small arched windows, and a balustraded parapet with red-domed kiosks.
  • The central bay standing forward with three arched windows and a gable in its red horseshoe hood, where the gilt Gajalakshmi sits between her elephants.
  • The central tower set back over the roof with its gilt dome and spire, and two grey domes on their kiosks.
  • At each end, two pink-brown granite towers with stacked oriels and crimson onion domes.
  • In front, the red-brick drive between green hoop railings, globe lamps and beds of red flowers.
Before After

Other monuments that got the most

More than forty monuments were improved. Here are some of the biggest changes.

Meenakshi Temple went from about 600k triangles to close to 800k on desktops. Its two shrine halls stand on moulded bases with pilasters, a curved eave and a parapet of miniature shrines. The Golden Lotus Tank has its pillared cloister. Every pillar in the corridors and the Thousand Pillar Hall has a base, a capital and a bracket. All fourteen gopurams have denser stucco figures.

Before After

Buland Darwaza: the arched recesses on the gate's two angled wings used to be placed sideways, buried inside the wall. They now face out towards the town in two tiers, each in a white marble border under merlons. There are also panelled piers, screened windows, muqarnas in the great iwan, and buttressed walls on the ridge.

The Jyotirlinga temples:

  • Trimbakeshwar and Bhimashankar have Nandi mandapas and deepmalas.
  • Grishneshwar's court, which had no entrance, has a gatehouse.
  • Kashi Vishwanath has blind arches, merlon parapets and a framed Ganga gate under gilt roofs.
  • Baidyanath has the red silk gathbandhan threads tied between Shiva's and Parvati's spires.
  • Mallikarjuna has a pillared porch, the gold flagstaff and a Nandi mandapa.
  • Somnath has its sea-wall promenade, the Baan Stambh (with its arrow pointing out to sea) and the Digvijay Dwar.
  • Kedarnath has Adi Shankaracharya in his pool, and Omkareshwar the Statue of Oneness.
Before After
Before After

Kerala and the south:

  • Padmanabhaswamy has Kerala gables, eave struts, a wall of oil lamps (vilakkumadam) lit at night and tiled coping.
  • Tirumala has a gilt sanctum, the Sampangi colonnade and the Neerazhi mandapam in its tank.
  • Ramanathaswamy has dressed walls and corridors.
  • The Shore Temple has a moulded base and water spout.

Jain sites:

  • Palitana and Shikharji have moulded shrines, doorways and manastambhas.
  • Soniji ki Nasiyan has pilasters, carved bands and cusped arches.

Forts and palaces:

  • Hawa Mahal has the white lime trim that outlines its pink façade.
  • Agra Fort has its river front and Khas Mahal.
  • Bekal has a cannon, magazine and temple.
  • Chittorgarh has ruined palaces and temples.
  • Fatehpur Sikri's Panch Mahal has carved columns.

Colonial and modern buildings:

  • Victoria Memorial and CSMT have their allegories, and CSMT's gate piers were lengthened to hold the lion and tiger.
  • India Gate has Netaji under the canopy, and the National War Memorial its Lion Capital.
  • The Lotus Temple has panels, ribs and copings on its petals.

An 800k budget, spent on buildings

From the start, every monument had to stay under 650,000 triangles on desktops and 300,000 on phones. With this much new detail, the temples ran out of room first and then everything else did. The desktop budget is now 800,000 for every monument. Phones stay at 300,000.

The important part is what the extra 150k may be spent on. Trees and ground cover are still planted only up to 650k, so the extra room goes to the architecture and not to more palm trees:

// The budget is for the buildings: trees and ground cover are planted only up to PLANT,
// 650k on desktops, so the extra goes to the architecture.
export const BUDGET = { high: 800000, low: 300000 };
export const PLANT  = { high: 650000, low: 300000 };

export function budgetFor(m, level = detail.level) {
  return BUDGET[level];
}

Phones keep the plain masses: the fine heads, carved jambs, ship fittings and arrow slits are desktop-only, and phones get coarser statues, light robed allegories and every other car. Every monument is still built at both levels and counted by a budget checker that fails if anything goes over. For example, the rebuilt Mysore Palace comes in at 509k on desktops and 290k on phones, and the Victoria Memorial at 651k and 277k. Other checks catch flickering surfaces (two faces fighting over the same plane) and buildings that come out taller than the real thing.

What's next

The pattern that worked here was to look at photographs, find what's missing, and put anything more than one building needs into the shared kit. For the statues it went one step further: every one was set beside its photographs and corrected until the pose, the clothes and the proportions matched, and the stand-ins borrowed from the kit were replaced. The next step is to do the same for the buildings that are still closer to massing models than to the photograph, the way Mysore Palace was rebuilt here.

If you like the project, a ⭐ on the GitHub repo helps other people find it.

Further reading in the repo:

  • components.md: every shared part and every statue, with a picture
  • architecture.md: how the code is organised
  • how-it-is-drawn.md: budgets, instancing, loading and the desktop and phone differences
  • monuments.md: all 101 monuments, state by state

Which monument, statue or animal still looks least like itself to you? Tell me in the comments.

articles.title: My password generator used crypto.getRandomValues and was still wrong 15% of the time
articles.description: My site has a small client-side password generator. It has a length slider, four checkboxes (A–Z,...
articles.body_html:
My site has a small client-side password generator. It has a length slider, four checkboxes (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, symbols) and crypto.getRandomValues. I assumed it was done. Then I went back to it while writing a blog post, and it had two problems. One was mostly theoretical. The other was very practical.

The original code 

let s = '';
if (up.checked) s += 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
if (lo.checked) s += 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz';
if (nu.checked) s += '0123456789';
if (sy.checked) s += '!@#$%^&*()-_=+[]{};:,.?';

const a = new Uint32Array(L);
crypto.getRandomValues(a);
let p = '';
for (let i = 0; i < L; i++) p += s[a[i] % s.length];

It uses a cryptographic RNG, so it looks fine. Here's what's wrong with it.

Problem 1: "Password must contain a number"

Ticking "0–9" only means digits are allowed. Nothing guarantees one shows up. With all four groups ticked, the combined set has 85 characters, and only 10 of them are digits.

I simulated 200,000 passwords at each length and counted how many were missing at least one of the ticked groups:

Length Missing a ticked group
6 70.6%
8 51.0%
12 26.5%
16 (my default) 14.6%

So roughly one in seven passwords at the default length would be rejected by a sign-up form that requires "at least one number and one symbol". The user ticked the boxes, copied the password, and the website said no. That's a real bug, not a theory.

Problem 2: modulo bias

a[i] % s.length maps 2³² possible values onto 85 characters. 2³² isn't a multiple of 85 (the remainder is 1), so one character gets picked very slightly more often than the others. Here the difference is about 2 in 10 billion, which nobody will ever exploit. But the fix is three lines, and it matters more when the set size is large relative to the random range. So:

// unbiased integer in [0, n)
function rnd(n) {
  const lim = Math.floor(2 ** 32 / n) * n;   // largest multiple of n
  const b = new Uint32Array(1);
  do { crypto.getRandomValues(b); } while (b[0] >= lim);
  return b[0] % n;
}

This is rejection sampling: throw away the few values from the incomplete top range and draw again. For small n a retry almost never happens.

The fix for problem 1

Pick one character from each ticked group first, fill the rest from the combined set, then shuffle so the guaranteed characters aren't always at the start:

const sets = [];   // only the ticked groups
// ...push each ticked group's characters...
const all = sets.join('');

const c = sets.map(g => g[rnd(g.length)]);   // one from each group
while (c.length < L) c.push(all[rnd(all.length)]);

for (let i = c.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {     // Fisher–Yates
  const j = rnd(i + 1);
  [c[i], c[j]] = [c[j], c[i]];
}
const password = c.join('');

I ran 20,000 passwords of length 6 with all groups ticked through the new version. All 20,000 contained every group.

Does guaranteeing one of each make the passwords weaker? Slightly, in theory, because the space is a little smaller than "any 16 of 85". In practice it's negligible. A 16-character password with all four groups is still around 100 bits of entropy, and the alternative is a password the website refuses.

The lesson

Using crypto.getRandomValues makes a generator secure. It doesn't make it correct. The bug that hurt users was in the logic around the RNG: what the checkboxes promise versus what the code guarantees. If you've written a generator like this, run a quick simulation over its output. It takes five minutes.

The generator is part of 14FreeTools, a set of free tools that run entirely in the browser. Nothing you generate is sent anywhere.

articles.title: 61 Hackathons, 2,000+ GitHub Contributions: The Free Chrome Planner That Keeps Me Shipping
articles.description: We have all been there.  You sign up for one hackathon. Then a friend sends another one with a cool...
articles.body_html:
We have all been there.

You sign up for one hackathon. Then a friend sends another one with a cool theme. Meanwhile, you still have a side project and a regular work sprint. On paper, everything looks doable — until two deadlines land in the same week, your weekends disappear, and you realize you haven't had a single real day off all month.

Regular calendars are great at showing when things happen, but they never stop you from overbooking yourself. They don't care if two sprints collide or if your rest buffer drops to zero.

So I built Dev Cadence — a free, open-source Chrome Side Panel extension I use every day to plan my own sprints, hackathons, and rest days.

No accounts. No subscriptions. No tracking.

Why I built this

If you check my profile, you'll see I've participated in around 61 hackathons across Devpost, DEV.to, DevSpot, NASA and other platforms. For a long time, I tried tracking everything in Excel and regular calendars — Excel gave me dates without a visual picture, and calendars never gave me a quick color-coded view of my actual sprint load.

I wanted a small control center for work that has a real start date, end date, and deadline, where I could open it for 2 seconds and immediately know: what's busy, what's free, and can I realistically take on another sprint?

On October 1, 2026, I built the first version of Dev Cadence for myself as a Chrome Side Panel extension. Here's the live stream review of the first version where the hosts broke down the design. I used it every day through October and November, writing down every rough edge I ran into.

In October, putting all my hackathons into those color-coded cells gave me a reality check: I had zero rest days and no space for other work — no way to ship a quality MVP like that. If you do want automatic deadline extraction and sprint pace advice, you can download Chrome's ~4 GB on-device Gemini Nano model in one click so prompts stay local on your device — or let the extension fall back to cloud Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

Why Projects Stall (and How Dev Cadence Evolved)

I hold a Master's degree in Management and Administration, so I pay close attention to why good projects stall. Across hackathons and side projects, I kept seeing the same gap: tons of people register with great ideas, yet very few actually cross the finish line. Usually it's not a lack of coding skill — it's not seeing the big picture of your own schedule while you're deciding what to take on.

With 2,000+ GitHub contributions over the past year while building under tough everyday conditions, I'm my own strictest test user. If you're curious to see how the extension evolved from a simple local tracker into a Hybrid AI planner:

What Dev Cadence does

Because it lives in the Chrome Side Panel, you can open it right next to any hackathon page, GitHub repo, or issue tracker without switching tabs.

  • Spot date overlaps immediately: When two sprints land on the same days, calendar cells split diagonally in both colors so you see the collision at a glance.
  • Protect your rest days: A bottom capacity bar tracks your month in real time — Build, Free, and Rest days against your personal monthly rest goal.
  • Stop copy-pasting deadlines: Open any event or project page, click Extract from Page, and Dev Cadence reads the active tab on demand to fill in the title, URL, and deadline for you.
  • Get a friendly nudge when you overbook: When sprints overlap or your rest days dip below target, the AI Pace Advisor gives a short, human reminder on what to prioritize first — and when to take a breather.
  • Transparent & under your control: Every AI response clearly shows an On-Device or Cloud badge, and you can stop generation or switch back to manual entry anytime.
  • Clean daily workspace: Card and Table tracker views, monthly pace analytics, 3 themes (Warm Vellum, Obsidian Brass, Ocean Slate), and font size scaling.

articles.title: Resurrecting HyperCard for the browser with Kiro — PhantomCard
articles.description: For Kiroween 2026 — AWS's spooky-season hackathon — I built PhantomCard: a resurrection of Apple's...
articles.body_html:
For Kiroween 2026 — AWS's spooky-season hackathon — I built PhantomCard: a resurrection of Apple's HyperCard that runs entirely in your browser. Stack of cards, buttons, fields, a working HyperTalk interpreter, System-7 monochrome chrome — no build step, no dependencies, just ES modules.

Try it live: https://till3005.github.io/phantomcard/ · Code: https://github.com/Till3005/phantomcard

Why HyperCard, and why "resurrection"?

Kiroween's Resurrection category asks you to bring dead technology back to life. HyperCard (1987) was the first mass-market hypermedia tool: a stack of "cards" holding buttons, fields and paint, scripted in HyperTalk — English-ish code like answer "Hello" with "OK" and go to next card. Entire generations learned programming by clicking around someone else's stack. Apple killed it in 2004, and browsers never quite replaced the magic of "open a stack, flip through cards, tweak a button's script."

PhantomCard resurrects that loop: you can flip through bundled demo stacks (a welcome tour, a séance deck, a haunted-house adventure), then hit Authoring mode and add a button, type its HyperTalk script, and watch it actually run.

How Kiro shaped the build

This is where Kiro stopped being a code generator and started being a collaborator:

  • Spec-driven development. Before a line of app code existed, we wrote the spec in .kiro/specs/phantomcard/: requirements (data model, HyperTalk grammar surface, interaction modes), a design doc, and a task list. When the agent drifted — proposing a React scaffold or a build step — the spec pulled it back. Every judgment call I made later traced to a spec decision, not a chat message.
  • Steering rules. .kiro/steering/ holds the rules Kiro worked under: zero build step, ES modules only, System-7 visual fidelity, no dependencies beyond lz-string. Those constraints are the reason the app loads instantly on GitHub Pages and the codebase stays readable end-to-end.
  • The HyperTalk interpreter — the hardest part — was co-written with Kiro CLI: a lexer, a recursive-descent parser, and an async interpreter with re-entrant send/dispatch semantics. Kiro wrote the grammar tests that caught edge cases (e.g. item idx of omens after put c + 1 into c).

What's in the box

  • 512×342 canvas-rendered cards with dissolve transitions (faithful to the original)
  • Buttons, fields, paint layers, custom Chrome menus and dialogs — all monochrome System 7
  • A real HyperTalk runtime: handlers, put/get/go/answer/ask, item/line chunks, the number of cards
  • URL-shareable stacks (state compressed into the link via lz-string)
  • Three demo stacks authored as HyperCard docs: Welcome, The Séance Deck, The Haunted House

What I'd do differently

The trickiest bug: a "dissolve" animation re-fired on every render, not just card changes — the fix was a one-line guard on the card id, found by watching a screen recording of the app in frame-by-frame. Retro-faithful doesn't mean stateless.

PhantomCard is MIT-licensed and in the running for Kiroween 2026's Resurrection category. If you grew up on HyperCard — or never got to — go flip a stack.

articles.title: I built a bank statement PDF to Excel converter that runs in the browser and won't say "done" unless the balances add up
articles.description: Bank statements are a strange kind of PDF: they look like tables, but they are only text fragments...
articles.body_html:
Bank statements are a strange kind of PDF: they look like tables, but they are only text fragments placed at coordinates. Copy-paste mixes the columns, and most online converters upload your statement to their servers. I wanted the opposite: nothing leaves the browser, and the tool proves its own result.

The result is Relevo, a free converter aimed at French bank statements (it also reads a few English and German layouts): https://electrocorbeau.github.io/relevo/

How it works

  • pdf.js extracts the text items with their positions. Items are grouped into lines (same baseline, with a tolerance) and into cells (a gap wider than about 0.85 em starts a new cell).
  • Header words (Débit/Crédit, Paid out/Paid in, Soll/Haben, Solde/Balance…) give each column a role. Without a header, amount columns are clustered by their right edge, and the "amount + running balance" hypothesis is tested against the printed balances.
  • Amounts are integer cents. 1 234,56, 1.234,56, 1,234.56, 45,20-, (45.20) and 45.20 DR all parse to exact integers, so there are no floating-point surprises.
  • Multi-line labels, page breaks, several accounts in one PDF, recap tables printed after the closing balance: each has its own rule, and an amount found inside a label never creates a transaction.

The part I care about most: reconciliation 

opening balance + credits − debits === printed closing balance   // to the cent
  • Printed intermediate balances are checked line by line, which locates a gap.
  • If the gap equals a duplicated row, or twice the amount of one row (a debit read as a credit), the app says so and points at the row.
  • No opening or closing balance found → the statement is shown as not verifiable, never "verified".
  • Every ambiguity (unknown sign, guessed year, uncertain column) is flagged on the row; you can correct it inline and the check reruns.

Privacy

A strict Content-Security-Policy blocks every outbound request except a license-key check (the paid tier is not open yet). You can load the page, switch off your network and convert a statement.

Testing, honestly

I generated 39 synthetic statements: 14 layouts, word- and character-split text, two accounts in one PDF, page breaks, a recap after the closing balance, plus deliberate errors (a missing row, a duplicated row, a 0.01 € gap) and broken files (scanned, corrupted, truncated, password-protected). Result: 1 658 / 1 658 rows with exact amounts, dates and labels, and every deliberate error detected.

The limit is obvious: these are synthetic statements, not real ones, so I don't claim compatibility with any specific bank yet. When a statement fails, the app can export an anonymized layout model (letters → x, digits → 9, dates and structural words kept) so the parser can be fixed without anyone sharing their data.

Source code: https://github.com/electrocorbeau/relevo

If you try it on a real statement, I'd love to know the result shown ("verified" or "gap detected") and the bank. Please never attach a real statement anywhere.

articles.title: The "LGTM" Epidemic: Why Your Code Reviews Are Just Rubber Stamps
articles.description: Imagine this. It’s Tuesday morning. You’re sipping your coffee, feeling good. Then, the Slack...
articles.body_html:
Imagine this. It’s Tuesday morning. You’re sipping your coffee, feeling good. Then, the Slack notification hits: a P1 incident. Production is down.

You jump into the war room. Everyone is panicking. You dig through the logs, trace the stack trace, and finally find the culprit. It’s a stupidly simple bug. A missing null check. Or a wrong variable name.

Then comes the gut punch: you check the Git history. This code was merged two weeks ago. It had been approved by three senior engineers. The PR had a green checkmark. The tests passed.

How did this happen?

Because everyone just commented "LGTM" and moved on with their day.

We’ve all been there. I’ve been there. I’ve been the one who approved a 500-line PR in 45 seconds because I was rushing to my next meeting. But this "Looks Good To Me" culture is slowly rotting our codebases, and we need to talk about it.

The illusion of "Four Eyes"

The whole point of code review is to catch what the author missed. It’s supposed to be a safety net. But in reality, it often becomes a performative ritual.

Why do we do it?

  1. The Bottleneck Fear: Nobody wants to be the guy who blocks a release because of a minor naming convention. We feel pressured to approve quickly so the team can ship.
  2. Cognitive Overload: If you send me a PR with 40 changed files, my brain just shuts down. I can’t review that properly, so I just scan it and hit approve, hoping for the best.
  3. The "It Compiles" Mentality: If the CI/CD pipeline is green and the tests pass, we assume it works. We forget that tests only prove the code does what the author thought it should do — not what it actually needs to do.

The math of the "Rubber Stamp"

Let's look at the uncomfortable reality of how we actually review code versus how we think we do:

PR Size (Lines of Code) Average Review Time Actual Review Quality
1 - 50 lines 15 - 30 mins High. Real questions are asked.
50 - 200 lines 10 - 15 mins Medium. Major logic is checked, edge cases ignored.
200 - 500 lines 5 - 8 mins Low. Skimming for typos.
500+ lines < 2 mins LGTM. (Please just let me close this tab).

When a PR gets too big, the reviewer’s brain switches from "analytical" to "survival mode". We stop looking for logic errors and start looking for reasons to just approve it and move on.

A code review is not a proofreading session

Here is what a typical "LGTM" review looks like in the wild:

+ // Adding a new caching layer for user profiles
+ const user = await getUserFromCache(userId);
+ if (user) {
+    return user; 
+ }
+ // Fallback to DB
+ const dbUser = await fetchFromDB(userId);
+ await setUserInCache(userId, dbUser);
+ return dbUser;

The Reviewer: "LGTM 👍" (Approved).

What the reviewer missed: dbUser could be null if the user doesn't exist, which means we are caching null and returning it, causing a silent failure on the frontend three calls later.

The author had all the context in their head, so it looked fine to them. The reviewer just glanced at the syntax, saw that it "makes sense", and approved it.

How do we fix the "LGTM" epidemic?
I don't think the answer is "just be more careful." That's like telling someone to "just be happier." We need structural changes.

1. Ban the LGTM comment.
Seriously. Make it a team rule. If you are approving a PR, you must leave a comment explaining what you checked. Even if it’s just: "Checked the DB calls and the error handling looks correct. Tested locally, works as expected." This forces the reviewer's brain to actually engage with the code, even for a few seconds.

2. Enforce the 200-line rule.
If a PR is over 200 lines of actual logic (excluding generated files, lockfiles, etc.), it gets rejected automatically. It must be split. Reviewing smaller chunks is the only way to maintain quality without burning out your seniors.

3. Ask a real question.
The best code reviews are the ones where the reviewer asks, "Why did you choose this approach instead of X?" or "What happens if this API call times out?" If you can't think of a single question to ask about a PR, it probably means you didn't read it carefully enough.

4. The "Rubber Duck" review.
Before you assign a reviewer, explain your own PR in the comments. Write a short paragraph: "Hey, this PR does X. The tricky part was Y, so I handled it by doing Z. Please pay special attention to the database transaction on line 45." This guides the reviewer exactly where to look and prevents them from getting lost.

It’s about culture, not tools
You can have the fanciest CI/CD pipeline, the most strict linters, and the best AI code review bots (yes, even Claude or Copilot). But if your human reviewers are just acting as a human LGTM button, your codebase is a ticking time bomb.

Code reviews are not a gate to pass; they are a conversation about the code. And a conversation requires more than just saying "Looks good."

Let's discuss
I'm curious how other teams handle this.

Do you have a team culture where it’s acceptable to block a PR for a whole day just to ask questions?

What is your "hard limit" for PR size before you hit that reject button?

Have you ever caught a catastrophic bug in a review that the CI completely missed? What was it?

I'd love to hear your war stories. Because at the end of the day, the best code review is the one that prevents you from getting that 3 AM PagerDuty alert.

articles.title: I built a 3D open-world mythology game in the browser with just Three.js
articles.description: I'm a software developer, and for a while I'd been curious how far a browser could go with nothing...
articles.body_html:
I'm a software developer, and for a while I'd been curious how far a browser could go with nothing but Three.js and the Web Audio API. So I built a game to find out.

Devayan: The Ten Drops of Amrita is a free, open-source 3D action-exploration game inspired by Indian mythology. You free ten sacred sanctums on foot, awaken a flying Vimana (sky-chariot), and fly from the ground all the way to orbit to face an eclipse-lord.

🎮 Play it: GAME LINK
💻 Source (MIT): REPO LINK

The rules I set for myself

  • No game engine. Just Three.js.
  • No build step. Plain ES modules served as static files.
  • No external assets. Every model is built from geometry in code, and every sound is synthesized.

These limits kept the project small and made it deploy-anywhere. It's a handful of JS files and can be hosted on any static host.

Zero build tools

Browsers can load ES modules natively, and an import map lets import * as THREE from 'three' work without a bundler:

<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "three": "./libs/three.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module" src="./js/main.js"></script>

The one catch is that modules need HTTP, so python3 -m http.server is the whole dev setup.

Models without a modeling tool

Characters, temples, boats and the Vimana are all built from basic geometries combined in code. A low-poly, flat-shaded style hides the lack of detail and keeps a large world light enough for the browser. A big part of the charm comes from lighting and color choices, not mesh complexity.

Music without audio files

I wanted the world to feel Indian, which meant a tanpura drone and bansuri flute melodies, plus temple chimes and combat effects. Instead of shipping audio files, everything is generated in real time with the Web Audio API. That keeps the download tiny and lets the music be generated live. It was the most fun part of the project.

Flying from the ground into space

I didn't want a loading screen between the world and orbit. The sky blends from day into space as you climb, using a blend factor based on altitude:

const spaceBlend = THREE.MathUtils.clamp(
  (vehicle.position.y - 28) / (spaceAltitude - 28), 0, 1
);

That one value drives the sky color, fog and the switch into the orbital combat arena, so the transition feels continuous.

Game design wrapped around a story

The ten sanctums, three unlockable "astras" and the orbital boss all come from one simple legend: ten drops of divine nectar, an eclipse-demon who wants them, and you in between. Having a story gave me an answer every time I wasn't sure what to build next. Progress is saved in localStorage, with an atlas for fast travel between freed sanctums.

What I'd do next

There's plenty to improve, and I'd love your thoughts:

  • Bridges or clearer paths early on, since water can block new players
  • A more convincing space environment when you reach orbit
  • A second phase for the boss fight
  • Performance testing across low-end laptops and phones

Try it and tell me what you think

The game is free, ad-free and open source. If you play it, I'd really like to hear about performance on your device and how the controls feel. And if you want to read the code, everything is in the repo.

articles.title: Your Sticky Header Is Hiding Anchor Links. `scroll-margin-top` Fixes It.
articles.description: Clicking a table-of-contents link lands the heading right behind your sticky nav, half-hidden. The fix isn't a JavaScript scroll offset — it's one CSS property the browser already checks before it scrolls.
articles.body_html:
You redesign a docs page. Sticky header, clean table of contents down the side, the kind of polish that makes a demo look finished. Then someone clicks "Installation" in the TOC, and the page jumps — except the "Installation" heading is now sitting behind the header, top third clipped off, like the scroll stopped one beat too early.

It's not a bug in your heading. It's not a bug in the TOC link. The browser scrolled exactly where you told it to. You just never told it about the header.

The obvious fix that didn't quite work

The TOC links are plain anchors: <a href="#installation">. The browser handles the jump on its own — no JavaScript required, which is exactly why it feels like it shouldn't need any. So the first fix is the one that feels native to the problem: intercept the click, do the math yourself.

document.querySelectorAll('a[href^="#"]').forEach((link) => {
  link.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const id = link.getAttribute("href").slice(1);
    const target = document.getElementById(id);
    const headerHeight = document.querySelector("header").offsetHeight;
    window.scrollTo({
      top: target.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY - headerHeight - 16,
      behavior: "smooth",
    });
  });
});

It works. Click a TOC link, the heading lands below the header, clean. Ship it, close the ticket.

Then QA files three more:

  • Deep-linking straight to yoursite.com/docs#installation — no click ever fired — still lands the heading behind the header, because the hack only runs on click.
  • The browser's native back/forward button restores the old scroll position, not yours — hitting Back after a TOC click snaps right back behind the header.
  • Mobile ships a taller header. headerHeight was read once on load; resize the window and the offset is stale until a reload.

Each of those is a separate bug with a separate fix — handle DOMContentLoaded for the deep-link case, listen for popstate, re-read offsetHeight on resize. You're not patching one bug anymore. You're reimplementing the browser's own "scroll to this element" logic, one missed case at a time, in a <script> tag.

The browser already asks "how much space do you need"

Fragment navigation, Element.scrollIntoView(), and the browser scrolling a focused element into view as you tab through the page all go through the same question: what counts as "this element is now in view"? Since 2021, every major browser has agreed on an answer CSS checks before any of them run — scroll-margin-top and its counterpart, scroll-padding-top.

Put it on the headings themselves:

h2,
h3 {
  scroll-margin-top: 4.5rem; /* roughly the header's height, plus breathing room */
}

That's it. No click handler, no preventDefault(), no recomputed pixel offset. Click a TOC link, hit the browser's native back button, paste a #installation link straight into the address bar — every path the browser uses to bring that heading into view now stops 4.5rem early, because the browser itself is doing the arithmetic, the same way it always has.

Per-heading vs. whole-page: pick the one that matches the bug

scroll-margin-top goes on the target — the thing being scrolled to. scroll-padding-top goes on the scroll container — usually html, or whatever element actually scrolls — and applies the same offset to every target inside it, without touching each heading individually:

html {
  scroll-padding-top: 4.5rem; /* one declaration, covers every #anchor on the site */
}

If every page on the site sits under the same sticky header, scroll-padding-top on html is the one-line, whole-site fix — set it once, forget it. Reach for scroll-margin-top on specific elements instead when different targets need different offsets: a shorter mobile header, a taller "in-page alert" banner above certain sections, or a card in a horizontally-scrolling carousel that needs its own left-edge margin rather than a top one.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stop hardcoding the header's height as a magic number

4.5rem is a guess that goes stale the day someone adds a banner to the header. Read the header's real height instead, and feed it in as a custom property:

:root {
  --header-h: 64px; /* kept in sync with the header's actual rendered height */
}

h2,
h3 {
  scroll-margin-top: calc(var(--header-h) + 16px);
}

const header = document.querySelector("header");
const setHeaderHeight = () =>
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--header-h", `${header.offsetHeight}px`);

setHeaderHeight();
new ResizeObserver(setHeaderHeight).observe(header);

Now the only JavaScript left is measuring the header — not re-deriving the browser's entire scroll-to-element behavior. If the header grows a second row on mobile, ResizeObserver catches it and the custom property updates; scroll-margin-top reads the new value on the next scroll. The division of labor is the point: JavaScript's job shrinks to "report one number," and CSS's job — "stop scrolling here" — stays where the browser already does it for free.

Where this still needs a human

scroll-margin-top fixes where the page lands. It doesn't fix a heading that's visually ambiguous about whether it's "the current section" once it's sitting right under the header edge — that's a design question about header contrast and spacing, not a CSS-property question. And if your TOC also needs to highlight the active section as the reader scrolls, that's a separate job (usually IntersectionObserver), not something scroll-margin-top does for you. It solves exactly one problem — stopping short of the header — and it's worth not asking it to solve the other two.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The bug report wasn't "the table of contents is broken." It was "the browser doesn't know about your header" — and it turns out the browser was willing to be told, in CSS, for free, since before most of us noticed. Got a scroll offset hack sitting in a click handler somewhere? Go check what it's actually compensating for — there's a decent chance one property replaces it.

articles.title: A VS Code extension to turn ANY free chatbot website into an AI agent (kind of)
articles.description: If you've ever pasted ten files into ChatGPT, asked for a fix, then manually copied the result back...
articles.body_html:
If you've ever pasted ten files into ChatGPT, asked for a fix, then manually copied the result back into ten different files by hand, this post is for you!

Already using ReptClip? Skip the intro and jump straight to what's new in v2.0

The problem

Coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor are great, but they cost money, and not everyone wants (or can afford) a subscription. Meanwhile, free chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude.ai are sitting right there, perfectly capable of writing good code, as long as you can get your project's context in front of them and get the resulting changes back into your files without losing your mind 🤔

That gap, pasting context in and applying diffs back out, is tedious enough that most people just don't bother. They either pay for an agent or they give up and do it manually, file by file.

Enter ReptClip

ReptClip is a free, open source VS Code extension that closes that gap 🙂 It lives right in VS Code's bottom panel, as its own tab next to your terminal, so there's no separate window or webpage to juggle. No API key, no subscription, no vendor lock-in. It works with literally any free chatbot you could find online.

Here's what the whole loop looks like in practice:

Here is the explanation. It's a 3-step process:

  1. Copy context to clipboard. Pick the files you care about (by path or glob pattern), hit the "Context" button, and ReptClip copies your project structure, AI instructions, and the file contents as clean Markdown straight to your clipboard (each section can be easily toggled on/off).
  2. Paste into your chatbot. Drop it into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, whatever you're using, along with your prompt.
  3. Apply the diffs. The chatbot replies with its normal explanation, along with a single code block containing Search/Replace diffs. Copy that block, click "Apply Diffs" in the ReptClip panel, and your files are updated!!! 😎

If the chatbot needs to see more of your project mid-conversation, it can ask for it, and you feed that back in with one more click.

Some things that make it safe to actually trust with your codebase:

  • ReptClip only touches files that are tracked by git. Anything your .gitignore files (at any depth) exclude is completely off-limits, for reading, searching, writing, creating, or deleting. .git folders are always off-limits too. Changing a .gitignore file always asks for confirmation first, since that can un-ignore something that was previously protected. If something ever goes wrong anyway, you can simply discard the changes with git.
  • Applying a diff is all or nothing. If one block fails to match, nothing gets written. Fuzzy matching handles whitespace and line-ending differences, but still requires a unique match.
  • You get 10 levels of Undo/Redo specifically for applied diffs, separate from your normal editor undo.
  • And MUCH more! 🙂 README

The UI state is saved per project automatically, so you don't have to re-enter when you come back or be mixed up with other projects.

How to install

It's available in both VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX. So no problem if you're on a VS Code alternative like Cursor or Windsurf. Simply search "ReptClip" and install.

What's new in v2.0

This is a major version bump. The headline feature is a complete rework of how ReptClip feeds extra context to your chatbot mid-conversation, and it also brings several useful new features for applying diffs 🎉

"More Files" is gone. Say hello to "More Context."

In v1, if the chatbot wanted more files, it would ask for a list of files. That's it. That's all it could ask for.

In v2.0, the chatbot can generate a small command block containing three types of commands, and ReptClip generates the output (no subprocess) and copies it to your clipboard!

  • cat <path> reads a full file.
  • grep <flags> <pattern> [paths...] searches your project's contents, ripgrep-style, running in-process (no subprocess spawned).
  • read-lines <path> <start> [end] pulls a specific, 1-indexed line range out of a file, handy for huge files where you only need a slice.

So instead of the chatbot blindly asking for whole files it might not even need, it can now search your codebase for the right TODO, grep for every usage of a function, or read just the relevant 20 lines of a 2,000-line file. It supports the flags -i, -w, -F, -g, -m, -v, and more. Everything still respects your .gitignore the same way the "Context" button does.

Click "More Context," and it works exactly the way "More Files" used to: read the clipboard, validate everything up front (so a bad path or invalid pattern fails the whole batch with a clear error instead of a half-built result), then build the output and send it back to your clipboard or output file.

Line counts in the project structure

The "Project structure" section now lists each file with its raw line count next to it, like src/main.py (387). This gives the chatbot a much better sense of file size before it decides whether to cat the whole thing or just read-lines a chunk of it. You can turn this off with the new reptclip.showLineCounts setting if you'd rather keep the structure listing minimal.

Move, rename, and explicit delete in diffs

The diff format your chatbot generates picked up two new one-line operations:

  • old/path.txt -> new/path.txt moves or renames a file without touching its contents.
  • old/path.txt delete removes a file outright.

That last one matters because the old behavior changed slightly: an empty REPLACE block used to mean "delete this file," but only if the SEARCH block matched the file's entire current contents. That meant deleting a file required the chatbot to regenerate the whole thing, verbatim, inside the SEARCH block, just to throw it away.

That's wasted tokens at best, and at worst a single mismatched character in a large file would make the whole delete fail to apply. Now the chatbot just writes old/path.txt delete and moves on, no regeneration needed! An empty REPLACE block on its own now just clears the matched text and keeps the file (even if that leaves it empty).

Undo now warns you before it steps on changes

If you hit Undo on an applied diff and the file in question has since been modified, either on disk or with unsaved changes in the editor, ReptClip now shows a warning first instead of silently reverting over your work.

And... I received my first external PR! 🥳

A huge part of making v2.0 safe to ship came from @mansio, who contributed two PRs to effessdev/reptclip, totalling roughly 1,500 lines of code!!! 🤯

The first PR focused on security in the diff-applying process. It uncovered several issues, including symlinks allowing writes outside the workspace, the ability to overwrite .git files, and Undo/Redo overwriting unsaved editor changes. It also fixed a .gitignore parsing bug.

The second PR caught even more edge cases, like missed editor changes on case-insensitive filesystems, race conditions during file updates, and incomplete symlink protection that could expose .git or .env contents to the chatbot. These are now fixed, huge thanks to @mansio! 🎉

A little help goes a long way 🥲

ReptClip wouldn't be quite what it is today without a few people who took the time to share their thoughts and suggestions.

A big shout-out to @unitbuilds for letting me know about the limited-time Qoder promotion. That tip made a huge difference and helped make ReptClip possible! The promotion may be over, but I now have something even better: ReptClip! 😁 In fact, I used ReptClip itself to build ReptClip v2. And I mean heavily! 🤯

Thanks to @piekwerk for actually giving ReptClip a try and suggesting that reverting changes should check for dirty editor tabs. I initially overlooked this, but now I get how important that was. In v2.0, both Undo and Redo now check for changes on disk and unsaved editor changes, warning you before proceeding.

And thanks to both @piekwerk and @mansio for pointing out something I hadn't considered: the order in which files are included in a prompt matters! Long prompts can lose effectiveness when important context gets buried in the middle. That feedback led me to make file patterns respect their written order, so you can push the most important files closer to the end of the context (right before your prompt).

For example:

  • **/*.py main.py: Includes all Python files, but puts main.py last.
  • **/*.py src/**/*.py main.py: Includes all Python files, puts files under src/ after the other Python files, and puts main.py last.

These might seem like small details, but they're exactly the kind of feedback that makes a project better. Thank you all for taking the time to help!

Try it out

Watch how beautifully ReptClip applies a large project reorganization:

Want to try it yourself? Head over to VS Code (or your favourite VS Code alternative), search for "ReptClip", and hit Install! It's that simple 😎

You can also find it on the official pages 🔥:

  • VS Code Marketplace
  • Open VSX Registry
  • GitHub repository

It's free, open source, and works with whatever chatbot you already have open in another tab. If you run into something weird while using it, please open an issue so I can fix it, or create a pull request if you want to fix it yourself 🙂 Reviews are fast right now! ⚡

If ReptClip saves you even one round of manual copy-pasting, or you think it'd be useful for others, the single most useful thing you can do for the project right now is head over to github.com/effessdev/reptclip and hit that ⭐ button! It's free, it takes two seconds, and it's the main way other people stumbling onto this post will know the project is worth a look!

articles.title: The Best Cyberdeck Is Not the Most Powerful One. It Is the One You Actually Carry
articles.description: Power looks great on a spec sheet. It looks terrible at the bottom of a drawer.     Everyone has seen...
articles.body_html:
Power looks great on a spec sheet. It looks terrible at the bottom of a drawer.

Everyone has seen that cyberdeck.

It is beautiful. It is huge. It has a mechanical keyboard that sounds like a thunderstorm, a 10 inch screen, three antennas, a battery pack the size of a brick, and enough RGB to be visible from low orbit. The build log took four months. The photos got 40,000 likes. The comments are all fire emojis and "this is the dream build."

And then it lives in a closet.

Not because it is bad. Because it is uncarryable. It is too heavy for a coffee shop. Too fragile for a backpack. Too conspicuous for a library. Too power hungry to survive a real afternoon away from an outlet. It was built to impress the internet, not to survive Tuesday.

Here is the uncomfortable truth the cyberdeck community does not like to admit: most cyberdecks fail the same way most gym memberships fail. Not from lack of ambition. From lack of friction math.

A cyberdeck is not a desktop. A cyberdeck is a companion. If you do not carry it, it does not exist.

The spec sheet trap

Spec sheets lie by telling the truth.

Yes, that Raspberry Pi 5 with NVMe is faster. Yes, that 16GB of RAM will crush a Pi Zero. Yes, that big display is easier to read. All true. All irrelevant if the thing never leaves your desk.

We have been trained by tech culture to worship maximums. Maximum cores. Maximum storage. Maximum screen. Maximum battery, in theory. But a portable device is not judged by its maximum. It is judged by its minimum viable hassle.

Ask a different set of questions:

How long does it take to go from "I have an idea" to "I am typing"?
How many cables, dongles, and adapters does it need?
Can you use it standing up?
Can you use it with one hand while holding coffee in the other?
Will you feel weird pulling it out in public?
Will it still be alive in three hours without hunting for a plug?

If the answer to any of those is no, you did not build a cyberdeck. You built a luggable desktop with extra steps.

The best deck is not the one that wins a benchmark. It is the one that wins the moment you decide to bring it.

Carryability is a feature, not a compromise

We treat small, light, and simple like apologies. Like we settled. Like we could not afford the real build.

Flip that.

Carryability is engineering. It is the hardest engineering in the whole project, because it forces you to make choices. A big deck lets you avoid choices. You just add more. More battery, more screen, more ports, more weight. A small deck forces you to decide what actually matters.

What do you actually do on a cyberdeck?

Be honest. Not the fantasy version where you are wardriving across the city while cracking Wi-Fi and live-streaming from a rooftop. The real version.

You take notes. You check a sensor. You SSH into something. You run a quick scan. You write a little code. You read documentation offline. You test a gadget. You journal. You mess around. You learn.

Almost none of that needs a flagship processor. Almost all of it needs instant on, good battery, a keyboard you can actually type on, and a screen you can read in sunlight or in a dim cafe.

The deck that does those five things every single day will teach you more, help you build more, and make you a better hacker than the monster deck that does everything in theory and nothing in practice.

Power is a party trick. Portability is a habit.

The three laws of a deck you will carry

After building, breaking, rebuilding, and abandoning more decks than I want to admit, I landed on three rules. They are not sexy. They work.

1. If it needs a bag, it is already losing.

The best cyberdeck fits in a jacket pocket, a small sling, or the side pocket you already use. Not a dedicated Pelican case. Not a backpack with a custom foam insert. Not a tote bag you have to remember.

The moment a device requires its own logistics, your brain starts negotiating. "Do I really need it today?" "It is kind of heavy." "I will just use my phone." And you lose. Every time.

A pocketable deck changes your relationship to it. You bring it because it is already there. You use it because the friction is zero. You find uses for it you never planned for, because it is present when life happens.

That is why the ESP32 handhelds and the Cardputer style builds punch so far above their weight. They are not trying to replace your laptop. They are trying to be there when your laptop is not.

2. Battery life beats processing power, every time.

A dead supercomputer is a paperweight. A live microcontroller is a tool.

People obsess over CPU and ignore the only spec that determines whether you get to use the thing: how long it runs, and how fast it charges.

A good carry deck should survive a full day of light use. Not "a full day if you turn the brightness down and do nothing." A real day. Notes, scans, terminal sessions, a little Wi-Fi tinkering, some idle time while you think.

That usually means you need to be ruthless about the screen, the radio, and the software. A smaller screen sips power. An e-ink or low-power LCD sips even less. Turning off Wi-Fi when you are not using it is not a compromise, it is a superpower. Running lean software instead of a full desktop environment is not primitive, it is smart.

The irony is that the "less powerful" deck often feels faster in the field, because it is awake, responsive, and ready. The powerful deck is still booting, still updating, still asking for a password, still dying at 34 percent.

3. It has to survive being used, not just being photographed.

Build photos are taken on clean desks. Real life is not a clean desk.

Real life is rain. Real life is a backpack full of cables that will scratch anything. Real life is dropping it on concrete. Real life is crumbs. Real life is a coffee spill. Real life is a friend picking it up and immediately pressing every button.

If your deck cannot survive that, it is a museum piece.

This is where the maker aesthetic actually matters. A 3D printed case with a little flex is better than a perfect CNC shell you are afraid to scratch. A screen protector you do not care about is better than a gorgeous bare screen you baby. A keyboard you can replace for 12 dollars is better than a custom keyboard you will cry over.

Build it to be scuffed. Build it to be repaired. Build it to be boring enough that you are not scared to use it.

The decks that last are not the prettiest ones. They are the ones with duct tape, a replaced screw, a slightly melted corner, and a story.

The fantasy build vs. the field build

Let us compare two imaginary builders. We all know both of them. We have been both of them.

Fantasy Builder starts with a parts list from a viral video. Pi 5, NVMe hat, 7 inch touchscreen, full size mechanical keyboard, RTL-SDR, big battery, 3D printed cyberpunk case with six antennas. Cost: 450 dollars. Build time: three weekends. Weight: almost 4 pounds.

He finishes it. He posts it. It blows up. He uses it twice at his desk to show friends. Then it goes on a shelf, because taking it anywhere feels like moving house.

Field Builder starts with a question: what do I want to do when I am away from my desk? Her answer is simple: take notes, run terminal stuff, test ESP32 sensors, and have something offline to tinker with.

She builds small. ESP32-S3 or a Pi Zero class board, a tiny keyboard, a small display, a 3D printed case that fits in her jacket. Cost: under 120 dollars. Build time: one afternoon. Weight: less than a paperback.

She carries it everywhere. To the park. To the bus stop. To work. She uses it to log sensor data on a walk. She uses it to sketch out a project while waiting for coffee. She breaks it, fixes it, upgrades one part at a time.

Six months later, who is the better hacker? Who has built more? Who actually understands their hardware?

It is not close. Field Builder wins, because she has six months of reps and Fantasy Builder has six months of dust.

Reps beat specs. Always.

What to actually prioritize

If you are building your first deck, or rebuilding the one that lives in your closet, here is the priority order that actually matters in the field. In order.

1. Keyboard and input.
If typing sucks, you will not write. If you will not write, you will not use it. A small but tactile keyboard beats a big mushy touchscreen every time. Test it. Type a paragraph. Type code. If your thumbs cramp in two minutes, it is the wrong keyboard.

2. Screen readability.
Not size. Readability. Can you read it outdoors? Can you read it at low brightness to save battery? Is the text sharp enough that you do not get a headache? A tiny sharp screen you can read beats a big washed out screen you squint at.

3. Battery and charging.
USB-C. Common cells. Easy to swap or top up from a power bank you already own. If it needs a weird charger, you will forget that charger. If it needs a weird battery, you will stop replacing it.

4. Durability and repairability.
Screws, not glue. A case you can reprint. Parts you can buy again. A design you can open without breaking. Your future self will thank you when something inevitably snaps.

5. Software simplicity.
One home screen. A few tools you actually use. Offline first. No 20 minute boot ritual. No dependency hell every time you turn it on. The best field software is boring, stable, and fast.

Notice what is not on that list: raw CPU power, RAM, storage size, number of ports, RGB, or antenna count. Those are nice. They are not the foundation. Build the foundation first, then add flair if you still want it and it does not break the first five.

The case for the "dumb" deck

There is a growing movement toward dumber, smaller, more focused devices, and it is not nostalgia. It is a reaction to bloat.

Your phone already does everything. It is a supercomputer with a great camera and infinite distractions. Your laptop already does everything else. What is missing is not another everything device. What is missing is a something device.

A deck that does one or two things really well, offline, without notifications, without an app store begging for attention.

An ESP32 anti-phone style handheld that is just for notes, terminal, and sensor tinkering. A BRUCE style tool that is just for wireless research. A biosphere deck that is just for watching a plant and learning about telemetry. These sound limited on paper. In practice, limitation is focus. Focus is what makes you actually finish a project instead of doomscrolling on a bigger screen.

The dumb deck respects your attention. It does not try to be your whole digital life. It tries to be a good tool for a specific kind of curiosity.

That is why so many of us end up loving the small builds. They do not compete with our phones. They complement them. They give us a place to think without being pulled into the feed.

How to rescue the deck you already built

If you already have a big deck gathering dust, do not scrap it. Shrink its job.

Take it apart, mentally. What is the one thing on it you actually loved? The keyboard? The screen? The radio? The battery setup?

Build a tiny version around just that one thing. Use the big deck as your home base station. Let it be the thing that flashes firmware, stores files, and does heavy work at your desk. Let the small deck be the thing that goes out into the world.

Most makers do not need one perfect deck. They need a system: a small carry deck, and a bigger home deck. The small one collects ideas and data. The big one processes them.

That is a much healthier way to think about it. You are not downsizing. You are specializing.

And if you are starting from scratch, start small on purpose. Start with the smallest deck that can do the thing you care about most. Use it for a month. Write down every moment you wished it did something else. Those notes are your real spec sheet. Not a YouTube video. Not a Reddit thread. Your actual life.

Build version two from those notes. Not from FOMO.

The real flex

The real flex in the cyberdeck world is not the most expensive build. It is the most used build.

It is the deck with the worn keys. The deck with the scratched case. The deck with the weird sticker and the replaced battery and the custom script that only makes sense to you. The deck that has been to the park and the bus and the basement and the cafe. The deck that has actually lived.

Anyone can buy parts and assemble a showpiece. It takes discipline to build something small enough, simple enough, and tough enough that you will actually carry it every day.

So ask yourself the honest question before your next build: am I building this to post, or am I building this to carry?

If it is to post, go big. Go wild. Have fun. No judgment. We all love a beautiful build log.

But if it is to carry, go small. Go simple. Go durable. Go boring in the best way. Build the deck that disappears into your pocket and reappears exactly when you need it.

Because the best cyberdeck is not the one with the best specs.

It is the one that is with you when the idea hits.

Keep building.

If this hit you in the chest a little, it is probably because you have a deck in a drawer right now. Go get it. Shrink it, fix it, or rebuild it smaller. Then actually take it outside.

For deeper build guides, field manuals, and hands-on projects, check the guides on Gumroad:

Relevant guides from numbpilled.gumroad.com:

  • Build a Pi 5 NVMe Field Cyberdeck for Kali, Recon, and Offline Work - https://numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/pi5-nvme-cyberdeck
  • Build a Raspberry Pi 5 Cyberdeck That Actually Survives Field Use - https://numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/pi5-cyberdeck-field-use

  • BRUCE Field Manual: ESP32-S3 From Zero to Field-Ready (Cardputer and T-Display-S3) - https://numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/bruce-field-manual
