articles.description: Previously   In the previous three Herdr practical articles (First time using Herdr, Using...
articles.body_html:
Previously

In the previous three Herdr practical articles (First time using Herdr, Using two agy Panes for record2gif, Writing my own Herdr mod: review-queue), I went from a single backend Code Review all the way to creating a macOS screen-to-GIF tool in one day, and even wrote a dedicated Herdr queue panel for my own workflow.

After validating the rhythm of "Claude Code as PM on the left, multiple Panes writing code in parallel on the right," this time I wanted to take a real-world, high-complexity topic used daily to stress-test this process:

Following a complete docs/PRD.md, build a Typora-style, single-window What-You-See-Is-What-You-Mean (WYSIWYM) macOS Markdown editor.

I named it Kalamos (Ancient Greek κάλαμος, a reed pen used for writing on papyrus)—the interface is like a quiet piece of paper, hiding Markdown syntax symbols when the cursor leaves. It is completely free, offline, requires no account, has no telemetry, and saves as clean standard GFM.

As a result, from starting work on 2026-11-19 to 2026-11-21, I completed all M1–M3 milestones within three days, accumulating 33 Issues and 38 merged PRs. I went from the project skeleton all the way to MIT open source, launched a four-language product page, and officially released v0.1.1.

The results first:

  • GitHub Repo: kkdai/Kalamos
  • Four-language Product Page: kkdai.github.io/Kalamos
  • Official Release Download: Release v0.1.1

I. What did Kalamos do? Tech Stack and M1–M3 Milestones

Before starting, I defined the tech stack, keeping the principles consistent with the PRD: Local-first, standard GFM, CJK-friendly, and fully offline.

Layer Tech Stack Description
Desktop Framework Tauri 2 (Rust) Lightweight macOS native shell, file system monitoring, secure saving, native PDFKit export
Frontend Core Vite + TypeScript Fast builds, combined with in-memory IPC mock for running dev and E2E directly in the browser
Editing Engine CodeMirror 6 + @lezer/markdown GFM base with custom math, CJK emphasis, front matter, and footnote syntax extensions
Math & Diagrams MathJax 3 + Mermaid (strict + DOMPurify) Fully offline SVG rendering; supports flow and sequence in addition to Mermaid
Other Components gemoji + Pandoc (Optional) Offline :emoji autocomplete; supports exporting/importing DOCX / EPUB / LaTeX if Pandoc is installed

Following the priorities in docs/PRD.md, the entire product was pushed through three milestones, eventually completing M1–M3:

Milestone Covered Features
M1 (Core Editing) Single-window real-time preview and source code mode (Cmd+/), lists and checkable task lists, links and heading bookmarks, GFM visual tables, 100+ language code blocks, offline MathJax formulas, inline image display and drag-and-drop paste, sidebar (file tree / file list / outline), Papyros / Melan themes and custom CSS, atomic saving (temp + rename) and crash recovery
M2 (Delivery) Native PDF export (including nested heading bookmarks, math, and diagram rendering), Pandoc multi-format export and import (DOCX / ODT / LaTeX / MediaWiki / EPUB), Mermaid / flowchart / sequence diagrams, image resizing and static blog root directory, YAML Front Matter / footnotes / [TOC], Ataraxia focus mode (F8) and Stichos typewriter mode (F9), word count and selection statistics
M3 (Optimization) Offline Emoji autocomplete, auto-pairing for CJK brackets and Markdown symbols, custom CLI image uploader (restricted to config file for security)

II. Multi-Agent Collaboration Mode: PM, Dual Worktrees, and "Seamless Switching when Quota is Exhausted"

The collaboration architecture this time followed the methods polished in previous articles but with stricter discipline, incorporating my own /herdr-pm and /herdr-coder skills:

  1. Left is Claude Code (PM / Reviewer): Reads PRD, breaks down Issues, defines interface contracts, reviews diffs, adds tests, runs validation. Only the PM touches git (create branch → commit → open PR → wait for CI → squash merge).
  2. Right has two coder Panes in Herdr (kalamos-a, kalamos-b): Each is bound to an independent git worktree (Kalamos.wt/a, Kalamos.wt/b). Files are completely isolated, using hc send / hc wait for asynchronous task assignment and reporting.
  3. Added a hygiene rule: This time I specifically required the PM to "Close the Pane once the work is done." After each task is merged into main, the PM executes hc kill + hc rm to clear the corresponding Pane, preventing the screen from becoming cluttered.

Practical Episode: What to do when the agy quota runs out?

When developing a large project halfway, a realistic problem is bound to occur: initially, both coder Panes were running agy (Gemini). After several rounds of major features, an Individual quota reached error popped up.

In a traditional single-tool workflow, you'd probably have to stop and wait for the quota to recover or restart the entire conversation context. But in Herdr, because the worktree is still there, the Issue specs are still there, and the PM's grasp of progress is still there, the PM simply replaced the exhausted coder with Claude Code (claude --permission-mode auto) in the same worktree to take over. The entire development pipeline continued without interruption.

This again validates the advantage of the TTT (Terminal Text Tool, AI Terminal Editor) pipeline discussed in the first article: Agents are swappable execution units; the process and state remain in the worktree, Issues, and the PM's hands.

III. The First Batch of "Landmines" Caught During User Testing (#49, #54, #56)

Just like with record2gif, after all features were done and unit tests were green, the real test was "me personally opening it to type a few words." Typing immediately caught three critical issues:

1. WYSIWYM was "not Typora-like enough" (#49, #54)

When I tried typing, I immediately complained: "A WYSIWYG editor should show Markdown effects directly. For example, - should immediately display as a list, and *test* should immediately become italic!"

The original implementation was too conservative; as long as the cursor was on a line, the syntax markers for the entire line were exposed. It felt similar to a dual-pane editor. After receiving the report, the PM didn't rush to create Issues based on imagination, but first used a Playwright script with a real keyboard to type and capture screenshots to reproduce the behavior. After confirming the exact behavior, it was split into two P0 Issues:

  • #49 (Block Markers): -, 1., - [], ##, > render into lists/headings/quotes immediately after typing a space. The source code is only exposed if the cursor is actually on the marker itself; pressing Enter on an empty list item or Backspace after a marker naturally exits the list or quote.
  • #54 (Inline Markers): *italic*, **bold**, code render and hide symbols the moment the closing character is typed. The source code only expands if the cursor is strictly inside the span; pressing Backspace behind a rendered span expands the syntax first before deleting, fully restoring the Typora feel.

2. Occasional CI Error: RangeError after IME Composition (#56)

Before and after adding GitHub Actions CI (#53), tests occasionally threw a tricky error:

RangeError: Position 55 is out of range for changeset of length 53

Tracing into the mapPos in blocks.ts revealed the root cause: in the StateField handling for footnotes, diagrams, and math, the IME composition branch was directly copying the old parsedTo instead of applying changes.mapPos to it. If the input method composition shortened the document length, the old position would exceed the end of the document, causing the next transaction's mapPos to explode.

The fix was solid: besides adding correct mapping to all three composition branches, I extracted src/editor/positions.ts so that all stored positions in the project follow the same protection layer:

export function clampPos(pos: number, length: number): number {
  if (!Number.isFinite(pos) || pos < 0) return 0;
  return pos > length ? length : pos;
}

export function mapPosClamped(changes: ChangeDesc, pos: number, assoc = -1): number {
  return clampPos(changes.mapPos(clampPos(pos, changes.length), assoc), changes.newLength);
}

Furthermore, the PM required the coder to first write a regression test that failed on the old code (3 cases each for vitest and e2e, then repeated with Playwright --repeat-each 20) to confirm the fix was green before allowing the merge.

IV. The Big Projects: The Reed Pen Icon and Splitting "Table WYSIWYM" into Parallel Halves

Once the core experience was stable, I threw in two requirements I cared about most: one was the "face" of the app (App Icon), and the other was the "final boss" of Markdown editors (Visual Tables).

1. Hand-written SVG Reed Pen App Icon (#58)

I wanted a beige-toned reed pen icon echoing the name Kalamos. Instead of installing extra image conversion packages, I had the coder follow a clean pipeline:

  1. Directly write a vector SVG: beige squircle base, diagonally placed bamboo pen barrel, slanted nib, and a drop of ink from the tip.
  2. Use the project's existing Playwright Chromium (scripts/render-icon.mjs) to render the SVG into a 1024×1024 transparent PNG.
  3. Run npx tauri icon to produce the macOS .icns and all sizes at once.
  4. The PM personally reviewed the 32px (Dock/small icon recognizability) and 512px previews before merging.

2. Table WYSIWYM (#59, P0): Design Assessment First, then Split into A/B Parallel Development

The original tables (#7) could render into HTML tables, but as soon as the mouse clicked in, the entire table reverted to | a | b | plain text source code, which was very jarring.

This requirement was large, so the PM split it into two sub-tasks with clear boundaries, assigned to kalamos-a and kalamos-b in parallel:

Part Responsible Pane Content and Contract
Part A (#61) kalamos-b Direct in-cell editing, updateDOM in-place updates, IME-safe write-back, keyboard navigation; Exports getActiveTableCell / focusTableCell for Part B to call
Part B (#62) kalamos-a Cmd+Opt+T insert dialog (with grid picker), `

Part A: Let the coder assess the technical solution before starting

I particularly liked one action by the PM: before writing the first line of code in {% raw %}kalamos-b, it was asked to evaluate: "Should in-cell editing use contenteditable spans or a nested CodeMirror EditorView for each cell?"

The coder eventually chose contenteditable spans for very clear reasons:

  1. CodeMirror automatically ignores DOM mutations inside widgets, preventing interference.
  2. Native browser contenteditable makes CJK IME composition incredibly smooth; text is only written back to the underlying Markdown on compositionend.
  3. All editing and structural operations go directly through the main editor's history, integrating Undo/Redo naturally.
  4. A 10×5 table would require 50 nested EditorView instances, which is too heavy for performance and memory.

Combined with updateDOM for in-place updates of non-focused cells, the entire table doesn't rebuild while typing, focus doesn't jump, and escapes for | ↔ \| and newlines ↔ <br> are handled correctly.

Part B: Pure function structural operations and shortcut conflicts caught by E2E

kalamos-a wrote all column/row insertion/deletion, alignment, and table deletion as table-ops.ts pure functions. Each operation is a single transaction (one Cmd+Z reverts the whole step). When writing back, it even calculates CJK full-width characters to auto-align the Markdown pipes.

A real-world episode occurred during development: the alignment shortcuts were initially set to Cmd+Opt+Shift+L / C / R. It turned out Cmd+Opt+Shift+R conflicted with the previously made "Clear Image Root" shortcut. Fortunately, the existing Playwright E2E tests caught this conflict immediately, and it was changed to the intuitive Cmd+Opt+Shift+← / ↑ / →.

Three "Devils in the Details" caught during Review

The two PRs for tables (#61, #62) caught three issues during the Review phase that are classic examples of "things you wouldn't think of just looking at specs, but only expose during testing":

  1. Typing <br> literally in a cell became a newline: The PM wrote a round-trip test and found that if someone wanted to write the instructional text "<br> tag" in a table, it actually broke the line when saved and reloaded! This was fixed so literal <br> is saved as <br>. A boundary condition where "an odd number of \ at the end of a cell escapes the pipe |" was also fixed by adding a space.
  2. Row drag handles pushed the first column out of alignment: Originally, the row drag handle took up layout width, causing the first column's content to be indented relative to the header. This was changed to absolute positioning, appearing only on mouse hover, making the table's vertical alignment instantly clean.
  3. Floating toolbar covered the heading above the table: When clicking into a table, the toolbar floating above it pressed directly against the previous line's heading. The fix was to dynamically reserve 38px of space above the table when active and synchronize scroll compensation to prevent the screen from jumping or the active cell from shifting.

By the time the tables were merged, the project had accumulated 353 vitest and 137 e2e tests, and the input latency for a 10,000-line benchmark p95 was 17–18 ms, well below the 50 ms budget set in the PRD.

V. Doc Writer Online, Catching a CSS Bug via Screenshots (#63), and "Why Not Open Another Writer?"

With the features complete, it was time to prepare the "face" of the product: I opened an independent doc-writer Pane (running agy + Gemini 4 Neon, attached to the Kalamos.wt/docs worktree) and assigned four tasks:

  • Rewrite the four-language README (English, Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Korean).
  • Create the four-language static product page site/ (referencing Typora's whitespace and large screenshot rhythm, but with original text, colors, layout, and images).
  • Write a Playwright IPC mock script to capture screenshots directly from the rendered App.
  • Add a GitHub Pages deployment workflow.

The PM reviewed two rounds and caught several flaws hidden in the details:

  • The feature and shortcut tables in the README were cross-checked against the code one by one.
  • In the HTML source code, newlines in the middle of Chinese sentences for layout caused an extra half-width space after CJK full-width punctuation in the browser; these were all cleaned up.
  • The GitHub Pages workflow added paths filtering to avoid redeploying the site every time the Rust code changed.
  • The hero screenshot on the homepage was changed to four versions (EN/ZH/JA/KO), so even the demo article in the screenshot changes with the language.

Unexpected Gain: Catching an App Layout Bug via Screenshots (#63)

The most interesting part was when doc-writer used Playwright to capture the first batch of App screenshots—I immediately saw something wrong: the text in the editing area was flush against the left edge of the window, and the sidebar covered the text when opened!

But editor.css clearly had .cm-content { margin: 0 auto; }? Checking the DOM solved the mystery:

CodeMirror 6's base theme dynamically injects .ͼ1 .cm-content { margin: 0; padding: 4px 0; } (CSS specificity 0,2,0), and it injects later than our own stylesheet, overriding our .cm-content which only had 0,1,0!

The solution was clean: instead of using the ugly !important, I increased the selector specificity to 0,3,0 and ensured that when the sidebar is open, its width is subtracted from the outer container, allowing the paper column to center automatically in the remaining space:

/* .ͼ1 .cm-content (0,2,0) injected later overrides simple .cm-content */
/* Use 0,3,0 to beat CodeMirror base theme without !important */
.cm-editor .cm-scroller .cm-content {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: var(--k-max-width, 720px);
  margin: 0 auto;
  padding-block: 56px 120px;
  padding-inline: var(--k-content-padding-x, 32px);
}

After PR #64 fixed this bug and added center-content.spec.ts, doc-writer re-captured all 9 images, and the interface immediately gained the "quiet piece of paper" vibe.

Management Decision: Should I open another Writer to share the load?

Writing four-language documentation and the product page took some time. Halfway through, I asked the PM: "Should we open a second writer to share the load?"

After assessment, the PM decisively said no, for very practical reasons:

  1. The work was entering the final stages.
  2. Two writers modifying the same set of README and site/ files simultaneously would only create massive merge conflicts.
  3. A new writer would have to re-read the entire codebase; the cost of re-familiarization was higher than just letting the original one finish.
  4. The tone and terminology across the four languages would become inconsistent.

Multi-Agent collaboration isn't "the more Panes, the better." Parallelize only when you can cut clean interface boundaries (like Table Part A/B); highly coupled finishing work is faster with a single dedicated Agent.

VI. Pitfalls: PM Errors, Open Source Checks, macOS Signing, and Final Bugs Caught Writing Blogs

Entering the open-source and official packaging phase, a series of pitfalls emerged that you "absolutely won't encounter unless you walk the last mile."

Pitfall 1: PM's own error—gh pr checks --watch disconnection fooled the merge gate

When merging Table Part A (#61), the PM followed the habit of using gh pr checks --watch to wait for GitHub Actions. Mid-way, a network connection reset occurred. --watch terminated early, and the PM didn't notice the CI was still running and clicked merge!

Although the main CI was green afterward and no disaster occurred, this was a process loophole. The PM changed habits on the spot: Never trust the exit code of --watch again; instead, use a loop with gh run view to explicitly check that status == completed and the conclusion is success before allowing a merge.

Pitfall 2: Transitioning from Private to Public Open Source and GitHub Pages

The repo was originally private. When preparing for GitHub Pages, we hit a GitHub free plan limit: private repos can't have Pages. The PM listed three options:

  1. Make the original repo public.
  2. Create a separate public repo just for the product page.
  3. Upgrade to GitHub Pro.

I chose to make the repo public. Before doing so, the PM scanned the entire git history (all 67 commits across branches):

  • Confirmed no API tokens, keys, or certificates.
  • Verified that test paths were fictional and didn't leak local environment info.
  • The only thing I had to approve was that the commit author email would be public along with the history. I confirmed it was fine, made it public, added the MIT License (#66), and deployed the four-language product page via GitHub Actions.

Pitfall 3: v0.1.0 → v0.1.1 and the macOS ad-hoc signature "Damaged" crisis

The first time I installed the packaged Kalamos.app into /Applications, running codesign -v immediately threw an error:

code has no resources but signature indicates they must be present

With such an incomplete ad-hoc signature, when others download the .dmg, macOS might jump straight to "The application is damaged and cannot be opened," not even allowing a right-click to open. Therefore, before releasing the v0.1.0 pre-release, I added re-signing and re-packaging the .dmg to the release process:

codesign --force --deep -s - Kalamos.app
# Then use hdiutil to repackage into .dmg

When fixing #67 and #69 for the v0.1.1 release, I used the same re-signing process. After confirming it worked, I deleted the old v0.1.0 pre-release and set v0.1.1 as the Latest.

Pitfall 4: When opening an .md from Finder, Kalamos was greyed out (#67)

After dragging the app into /Applications, I tried right-clicking an .md file in Finder and selecting "Open With," but Kalamos was greyed out and unselectable!

There were two reasons:

  1. tauri.conf.json didn't have fileAssociations set, so the packaged Info.plist lacked CFBundleDocumentTypes and the Markdown UTI declaration. macOS didn't know it could open .md files.
  2. Even if selectable, the Rust side hadn't handled the macOS RunEvent::Opened event, so double-clicking from Finder or cold-starting would result in nothing happening.

PR #68 fixed both: registered seven extensions (md, markdown, mdown, mkd, mkdn, mdwn, mdtxt) and the imported UTI net.daringfireball.markdown. When Rust receives an open event, if the frontend isn't initialized, it queues the event and processes it once the frontend is ready. Cold-starting with open -a Kalamos file.md was verified to work.

Pitfall 5: Using Kalamos to open "this blog" immediately caught broken ../images/ (#69)

The final bug felt particularly karmic. I finally used Kalamos to open the previous post on this blog (_posts/2026-11-15-herdr-review-queue-mod.md), and all ../images/xxx.png images showed "Failed to load image"!

The reason was that Tauri's asset protocol scope, for security, only allowed the folder where the document is located (i.e., _posts/). Jekyll blogs typically put posts in _posts/ and images in a parallel images/ folder. The path ../images/ was blocked.

But the fix couldn't be lazy by "allowing the entire parent folder" (if a user opens a file in their home directory, it exposes the whole folder to the WebView). PR #70 took a restrained approach:

  1. Added an allow_asset_file command in Rust: uses fs::canonicalize to resolve .. and symlinks, confirms it's a real file, and checks if the extension is in the image whitelist.
  2. After passing checks, only that specific image file is added to the asset_protocol_scope, never the entire parent folder.
  3. Before the frontend loads a local image not in the document directory, it calls allow_asset_file (with caching and a retry on failure). 
#[tauri::command]
pub fn allow_asset_file(app: tauri::AppHandle, path: String) -> Result<(), AppError> {
    use tauri::Manager;
    let requested = Path::new(&path);
    let canonical = check_asset_file(requested)?; // canonicalize + file check + image extension whitelist
    let scope = app.asset_protocol_scope();
    let to_err = |e: tauri::Error| AppError::new(crate::error::ErrorKind::Io, e.to_string());
    scope.allow_file(&canonical).map_err(to_err)?;
    if requested != canonical {
        scope.allow_file(requested).map_err(to_err)?;
    }
    Ok(())
}

After the fix, the PM verified it using the packaged App with the same _posts/ + ../images/ structure. Images loaded successfully, and I finally felt safe cutting the official v0.1.1 release.

VII. Final Acceptance Numbers and the Multi-Agent Collaboration Checklist Learned This Time

As of v0.1.1 (latest main), all automated defenses and benchmarks are green:

Check Item Result Description
Vitest Unit Tests 369 passed Covers parser, table-ops, positions, export, image logic
Playwright E2E 145 passed Includes real keyboard typing, tables, centering, IME stress tests
Rust cargo test 86 passed Atomic saves, file association queue, asset scope whitelist, and symlink protection
Rust Clippy 0 warnings cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
GitHub Actions CI All Green (macos-latest) Auto-runs tsc / vitest / build / cargo test / clippy / Playwright on every PR
Input Latency p95 17–18 ms 10,000-line long text benchmark, far below the 50 ms goal

I've summarized the experience of running a large project over these three days into an advanced Herdr Collaboration Checklist:

  • [ ] 1. Let the coder do a design assessment before writing code for complex features: Like comparing contenteditable vs. nested EditorView for tables, saving the cost of going down the wrong path.
  • [ ] 2. Split large requirements into "Interface Contract + Dual Worktree Parallelism": Part A exports getActiveTableCell / focusTableCell, allowing Part B to start simultaneously with almost zero merge conflicts.
  • [ ] 3. No need to stop when the quota is exhausted; switch models in the same worktree: When agy hit Individual quota reached, I immediately switched to claude --permission-mode auto to take over.
  • [ ] 4. Don't force a second Agent for finishing work: For highly coupled tasks like translation and product page finishing, a single dedicated writer is faster and more consistent in tone.
  • [ ] 5. Don't just trust gh pr checks --watch: Network interruptions can cause it to end early. Use gh run view to explicitly check status == completed before merging.
  • [ ] 6. Close the Pane when the task is merged: Develop the habit of using hc kill + hc rm to keep the Herdr window from being cluttered with idle terminals.
  • [ ] 7. Write a "fails on old code" regression test before fixing a bug: Like the IME out-of-bounds in #56 and the <br> round-trip in #59; it's only fixed when it turns from red to green.
  • [ ] 8. Screenshots and "opening your own real project" are the strongest acceptance tests: Screenshots caught the CSS specificity issue in #63; opening my own blog caught #67 and #69.
  • [ ] 9. Always check codesign and Info.plist before a macOS release: Verify the ad-hoc signature is complete and that file association UTIs and RunEvent::Opened are all connected.

Summary

Looking back at the evolution of these four Herdr practical articles, it's quite interesting:

  1. From fixing bugs to building a complete product: The first article fixed an existing backend, the second made a small tool, the third wrote a mod for the workflow, and the fourth took a complete desktop editor PRD (M1–M3) from zero to MIT open source and v0.1.1 in three days.
  2. Models are just slots; the process is the asset: When the agy quota ran out halfway through development, switching to Claude Code in the same worktree allowed for a seamless continuation. As long as the specs, contracts, tests, and git discipline are in the PM's hands, any model can take over.
  3. Beyond "all tests passed," you always need a real user's hands: If I hadn't typed personally, hadn't asked doc-writer to take screenshots, and hadn't used it to open the previous post on this blog, the issues in #49, #54, #63, #67, and #69—which most affect the user experience—would never have been caught by CI alone.
  4. The tool is finally back in my hands: Kalamos can now open the .md files of this blog directly from Finder and correctly load screenshots from ../images/. From now on, I can write articles using the editor I built together with the Agents.

Feel free to download and try it out, or visit the repo to browse or give it a star:

  • GitHub Repo: kkdai/Kalamos
  • Product Page: https://kkdai.github.io/Kalamos/
  • Official Release Download: Release v0.1.1

articles.title: Riemann Hypothesis Lean proof: what the checkers actually check
articles.description: A 17.4M-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis compiles. What Lean, nanoda, con-leche and lake comparator check, and what is still open.
articles.body_html:
The Riemann Hypothesis Lean proof that Levent Alpöge posted on November 20, 2026 is 17.4 million lines of code in 175,187 files, and it compiles. Strangers have built it, several independently written checkers accept the exported proof, and one check was still running when I last looked on Saturday afternoon (GMT+7). This post explains what each of those checks covers, what it leaves open, and what a developer can reuse from the way people are checking AI-written proofs.

Everything below is a claim under review, and no part of it is an accepted result yet. I use "claims", "compiles" and "accepts" on purpose.

TL;DR

  • Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a four-page note saying he believes he has, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization, and released only Lean code (note).
  • Andrew Sutherland of MIT reports that all 175,187 modules compile with zero errors, and that the five headline theorems use only the three standard axioms (MIT verification page).
  • Kernels written by other people accept the 61.6 GB export: nanoda in 27 minutes 42 seconds and con-leche in 3 minutes 15 seconds.
  • As of Saturday November 21, 17:05 GMT+7, the official lake comparator run on the full proof and the Lean kernel replays were still running. Its statement comparison and axiom check had passed in one run, and con-leche's compare mode accepted all five theorems.
  • Nobody has digested the argument yet. Terence Tao wrote that this will take some time.

What the Riemann Hypothesis Lean proof actually contains

Alpöge's note says Claude "flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line", and that a prose version he generated hit more than 250,000 pages, which he called slop. He posted none of it. What exists is a Lean archive split into 14 parts, about 239 MB compressed, 17,374,215 lines in 175,187 files according to the import analysis people posted on the Lean Zulip thread.

Lean is a proof assistant. You write a statement and a proof, and a small program called the kernel checks every step against a short list of rules. If the kernel accepts, the statement follows from the axioms you allowed. The Riemann Hypothesis here is Mathlib's own definition, which in Lean reads that every nontrivial zero of the zeta function has real part one half. Its doc comment in the library says that constructing a term of that type is worth a million dollars (Mathlib source).

Sutherland's page notes that "GRH" in this archive means Dirichlet L-functions only, so I avoid calling it the extended hypothesis.

Buzzard's four questions: what does a green Lean build check?

Nine days earlier, Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London published a checklist for exactly this kind of repository (Xena Project post):

  1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement?
  2. Does the code compile?
  3. Does the code prove the theorem as stated? His tool for this is lake comparator.
  4. Does the code exploit a bug in Lean's official kernel? His tool is lake comparator --paranoid, which uses several independent kernels.

Buzzard, who tried to compile Anthropic's 13 million line Fermat formalization in September and ran out of memory, writes that AI-generated code needs these tests before anyone makes a correctness claim. I covered that Fermat episode when it came out and stamped it SHIP IT; this one needs more review.

Question two: does it compile?

This is the easy one, if you own a big machine. Sutherland's page reports zero errors across all 175,187 modules and #print axioms output listing only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound for the five headline theorems. To run the official check yourself you need about 100 GB of memory, per the same page. Buzzard wrote on the Lean Zulip that the answer to this question is yes.

Question four: could the kernel be fooled?

Scott Aaronson points out that Lean's kernel has had bugs that allowed proofs of 0 = 1, and says those issues should be fixed urgently (his post). He also notes that so far none of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted, while several without certificates have.

The practical answer is to run more than one kernel. According to Sutherland's page, nanoda, an independent Rust kernel, accepted the full export in 27 minutes 42 seconds on 80 threads, and con-leche accepted it in 3 minutes 15 seconds on 64 threads. Joachim Breitner of the Lean community wrote that con-leche is backed by a consistency proof, and that the high-level summary is that this proof is now "very very thoroughly checked". lean4lean accepted every compiled module as well, with five modules needing a raised step limit.

Questions one and three: is it the right theorem?

These are the dangerous ones. The statement is short and trusted. The proof sits behind 17 million untrusted lines, and any of them could in principle redefine a symbol and prove something easier. That is what lake comparator is for: it checks that the theorem in a trusted file and the theorem delivered through the untrusted imports are identical, and that only the standard axioms are used. I explained the tool on November 10 in the episode about Google's checked proofs for Signal's code.

Where the comparator run stood

At the last update to the MIT page (2026-11-21 10:05 UTC, which is 17:05 GMT+7; the status rows were the same when I re-read the page at 21:29), the official lake comparator run on the full proof was listed as running. The page says its statement comparison and axiom check had already passed in one run, and that the slow stages replay the proof in Lean's default and paranoid kernels, single-threaded on a 62 GB export. Sutherland wrote on the Zulip that he did not expect it to complete before that night, more likely the next day.

Two other checks cover part of the same ground:

Check Status on the MIT page (17:05 GMT+7)
lake comparator end to end on the full proof running
Lean default and paranoid kernel replay of the export running, single-threaded
con-leche --compare, an independent implementation of Comparator's statement matching accepts all five theorems
Robin's inequality, a divisor-sum statement with no zeta in it, combined with an independent Robin formalization compiles; con-leche and nanoda accept

Robin's inequality says that for every n above 5040, the sum of divisors of n is smaller than e to the Euler constant times n times log log n. It is an old equivalent of the Riemann Hypothesis, so a proof that implies it without mentioning zeta tests the statement from another side. Sutherland wrote that this effectively rules out holes in the definitions used in the Mathlib formulation. His own page also says the result relies on the kernels and on Mathlib's definitions being what they are intended to be.

Status pages like this move quickly. If you are reading this later, go to the page rather than to my table.

The human-written rival and the unreadable proof

The same morning, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society, posted a draft general Riemann Hypothesis proof by Alessandro Masullo, written with no AI, which Brian Conrad had been reviewing for months (Vakil's post). About eight hours later Vakil added that several people had reported problems, found with the help of different AI models, and that he makes no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy. Conrad told Scientific American that the draft is undergoing major revision (SciAm).

One claim comes with a machine that says yes. The other comes with a PDF that people are arguing about. Neither is an accepted proof.

A compiling Lean file also cannot say why the argument works. Terence Tao wrote that the digestion process will take some time, though there is a human author to talk to (Tao's post). Aaronson says mathematicians will be satisfied when they can explain and reconstruct the ideas themselves.

What developers can reuse from this

  1. Read the specification before the code. A checker proves the statement you gave it, so look at who wrote the statement and how small it is.
  2. Ask what compares the proof to the statement. The comparator pattern, a trusted spec checked against what the implementation delivers, applies to any AI-written code.
  3. Run a second checker that someone else wrote. Several independent kernels agreeing is far stronger than one kernel agreeing with itself.
  4. Treat reproducibility as a property to test. Sutherland's page notes that the per-file hashes of the compiled files depend on the build directory, because Lean can store the source path inside them: 98,219 of the 175,187 compiled files contain it.

Scientific American notes that the result has no immediate real-world applications. Nothing in your stack changes tonight.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd ship the checking and hold the conclusion. The compile is real, strangers' checkers agree, the official comparator run was unfinished at the last update, and mathematicians have not yet digested the argument.

One market footnote: Anthropic's shares fell more than eight percent on Friday, from $97.17 to $88.91, in a sell-off The Guardian does not tie to the proof (The Guardian). I do not either, and this is not investment advice.

FAQ

Does a Lean proof that compiles mean the Riemann Hypothesis is proved?
It means the Lean statement follows from the allowed axioms according to the checkers used. Whether the Lean statement says what mathematicians mean, and whether the argument is understood, are the questions the comparator, the independent kernels and human review address.

What is lake comparator?
A Lean tool that checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved through untrusted imports are identical, and that only the standard axioms are used.

How long does it take to check the Alpöge proof?
On the MIT page, nanoda took 27 minutes 42 seconds on 80 threads and con-leche 3 minutes 15 seconds on 64 threads for the exported proof. Compiling the source took hours on large machines, and the Lean kernel replays are single-threaded and slower.

Is the Masullo proof correct?
Nobody has said so. Vakil makes no claim as to its correctness and Conrad says it is undergoing major revision.

Sources

  • Alpöge note (PDF)
  • Andrew Sutherland, MIT: RH Lean proof verification files
  • Kevin Buzzard, "...and the proof is checked in Lean" (Xena Project)
  • Lean Zulip discussion
  • Mathlib: RiemannZeta.lean
  • Ravi Vakil, Hurried Announcement
  • Terence Tao, What's new
  • Scott Aaronson, Shtetl-Optimized
  • Scientific American: claim, independent checks, dueling claims
  • The Guardian: Nasdaq and Anthropic's second day
  • Hacker News discussion

articles.title: Trimming Fixed the GitHub Shape. On the Web Shape It Costs You the Answer.
articles.description: helve_dev left a comment on my trimming piece that I could not shake. He had seen the same thing in a...
articles.body_html:
helve_dev left a comment on my trimming piece that I could not shake. He had seen the same thing in a different shape: web search and extraction results, full markdown and JSON payloads, making a small model anchor on whatever was longest or loudest instead of what answered the question. Trimming to the tight fields that actually carry the answer, he said, fixed accuracy and the token bill at the same time, and it mattered most on long loops, where old results pile up over 15 or 20 turns until the model is reading boilerplate instead of facts. He had watched it happen in real traces. He had never run a clean two-sided test with scored pass rates. So I ran one. The result is not what either of us expected.

The setup is the same shape as the GitHub run, moved onto the web. Twelve questions, five pages each, all written for this test. The model searches, reads pages, and answers with the exact value: a version, a price, a flag, a limit. One arm sees the full page text in the search results. The other sees only the title, the link, and the first 200 characters of each page, and has to open a page to read the rest. Six questions hide the decisive fact inside those first 200 characters. Six hide it further down, where only opening the page finds it. Same small model as before, same six-call limit, every arm run twice. Both second runs came back identical to the first, so I am counting 24 tasks per arm, not 48.

1. The accuracy gain does not travel. It reverses.

Full pages solved 22 of 24. Trimmed pages solved 20 of 24. On the GitHub shape, trimming nearly doubled the score. On the web shape, it costs two tasks.

Both tasks it loses are the ones where the fact sits past the cut. One asks the per-seat price of a team plan after a price change. The trimmed snippet shows the cheaper plan's price first ($8, for the solo plan), and the model answers $8 and never opens the page. The real answer, $12, is three sentences further down. The other asks which command flag skips the build cache. The snippet never shows the flag, so the model opens the wrong page, the caching guide, and answers with a cache command instead. The trimmed arm solved all twelve questions where the fact was visible in the snippet, and only eight of twelve where it was not. The full arm solved all twelve of the hidden ones.

That is the shape of the failure, and it is worth naming plainly. The model does not treat a snippet as a pointer to a longer page. It treats it as the page. When the visible text contains a plausible answer (another plan's price, a related command), it answers from that and stops. Trimming only helps when the trim keeps the answer. When it cuts the answer, the model does not go looking for it. It answers with whatever the trim left behind.

2. The saving is small, and the re-open eats it

Trimmed pages cost 513 tokens per turn against 556 for full pages, and 1,472 per task against 1,667. That is 12%, not the 63% the GitHub trim saved. Two reasons. First, the pages here are short, so the gap between a full result and a trimmed one is only about 70 tokens. Second, the trimmed arm opens pages more often (0.67 opens per task against 0.42), and every open drops a full page into the history. By the third turn, the trimmed arm's prompt is actually bigger than the full arm's: 791 tokens against 783. The saving exists on the first turn and is gone by the third.

This is the part helve_dev's traces got right and my test sharpens. The bill on a long loop is not set by the size of one result. It is set by what stays in the history. Every result the model sees stays there, turn after turn, and every page it opens to recover a trimmed fact stays there too. Trimming one result does not trim the history. It just moves tokens from the search result into the re-open.

3. Both arms balloon the same way

Turn one costs about 162 tokens in both arms. Turn two costs 722 for full pages and 651 for trimmed. Turn three costs 783 and 791. That is nearly a fivefold rise in three turns, whatever the payload size, because the history only grows. The trim does not bend the curve. It shifts it by one turn at most.

The honest limit here is that nothing in this test ran long. Every task ended in three turns, so the 15-to-20-turn loops helve_dev described never happened. The curve to turn three is real evidence; the curve to turn twenty is still his traces, not my numbers. But the direction of the evidence is against the trim: if the history grows fivefold in three turns in both arms, a longer loop does not fix that by trimming harder. It makes the re-opens pile up faster.

4. The two arms fail in opposite ways

The full arm's only failure is a question needing two facts, a version and a date. It answered the date and dropped the version. The trimmed arm solved that one, and all three two-fact questions. Short results seem to help the model hold two facts at once. That is three tasks, and I will not lean on it. But the pattern is neat enough to note: full pages cost you the second fact, trimmed pages cost you the hidden fact. Neither shape is free. The question is which fact your task hides.

So where does that leave helve_dev's claim? Half right, in a way that matters. Trimming does cut the bill on the web shape, a little, not a lot, and only until the model starts re-opening pages. And trimming does not fix accuracy here. It breaks it, exactly on the questions where the answer sits past the cut. The GitHub trim worked because every decisive fact sat inside the first 300 characters by design. The web does not promise that. A page puts the price of the wrong plan first and the right one third. A snippet is not a summary. It is the top of a page, and the top of a page is where the least important facts live.

The fix I am keeping is narrower than the one I went in with. Trim the search result, yes, but only when the snippet is built to carry the answer, not just the first 200 characters of whatever the page happens to start with. And if the answer might sit past the cut, the model needs a reason to open the page before it answers, not permission to. A snippet that shows a plausible wrong answer is worse than no snippet at all, because the model will take it and stop.

Have you watched a small model answer from a snippet instead of opening the page? What made it open the page — a better snippet, a different instruction, or just a bigger model? I am curious what worked, because trimming alone did not.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Mingle (MIT): Bring Your Local Coding Agents into Slack, Discord, Telegram & More — With Zero Servers
articles.description: Bringing your own coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi Code, etc.) into custom...
articles.body_html:
Bringing your own coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi Code, etc.) into custom tooling is pretty common now. What still bothered me about most agent-to-IM bridges was the cloud relay: if a third-party server sits between your chat apps and your agent, your private work conversations pass through someone else's infrastructure—bringing both the risk of a server breach and the risk of your data being logged or sold.

So I built Mingle (MIT-licensed)—a zero-server desktop app that lets you bring your local coding agents directly into the chat apps you already use: Slack, Discord, Telegram, iMessage, WeChat, Feishu/Lark, WeCom, DingTalk, QQ, and GitHub Issues/PRs.

Why zero-server matters

Mingle has no backend service at all:

  • No Mingle server, no accounts, no telemetry.
  • Direct platform connections: connects straight to each chat platform's official bot interface (or your local Apple ID for iMessage)—never routed through a hosted Mingle relay.
  • Localhost-only surface: the local console and API bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
  • OS keychain for secrets: bot tokens and credentials stay inside macOS Keychain, Windows DPAPI, or Linux Secret Service.
  • Plain-file memory: each agent's persona and memory are ordinary files in a local folder (ROLE.md, MEMORY.md, and notes/).
  • Optional 24/7 mode on your own hardware: if you want your agent online when your laptop sleeps, you can deploy the runtime to your own SSH host directly from the app—still your machine, no middleman.

What makes it usable in real chats

Connecting a CLI agent to a webhook is easy to demo; making it behave well in daily group chats took most of the real engineering:

  1. One agent, unified memory across chat apps The same agent can join your Slack workspace, Discord server, and Telegram/WeChat groups while sharing one continuous memory. You can ask it in one app what was decided in another, or ask it to forward a summary across platforms.
  2. Parallel side tasks without blocking chat When you hand it heavy work—writing code, investigating a bug, running long shell commands—it forks the work into a background task (opening native threads in Slack, Discord, and Feishu) while staying responsive in the main room.
  3. Group-chat etiquette It listens passively, responds when addressed by name or nickname without needing an @ on every message, and automatically throttles itself in busy channels instead of spamming every turn.
  4. 14 coding-agent harnesses + one-click session handoff Supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Kimi Code, Cursor, and 9 more harnesses via OAR. You can also hand off an existing session's context and preferences into a Mingle agent in one click.

Honest current status

Mingle started about a week ago and is currently at v0.4.8—definitely early:

  • End-to-end verified harnesses: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Kimi Code.
  • Chat platforms: Feishu is battle-tested on a live tenant; the other connectors are currently verified against platform APIs and automated tests.
  • Installers: macOS (Apple-signed & notarized), Windows (unsigned for now), Linux, plus a one-line install script.

Links

  • GitHub (MIT): https://github.com/earayu/Mingle
  • Website & docs: https://mingle.build

If you try it out, I'd love feedback on the zero-server architecture, the SSH deployment flow, or any quirks you hit with a specific chat platform—feel free to drop a comment here or open an issue on GitHub.

articles.title: The Comment That Ruined My Thursday
articles.description: 09:12. I open the pull request and there it is, three words under a line of my code, in red.  "This...
articles.body_html:
09:12. I open the pull request and there it is, three words under a line of my code, in red.

"This is wrong."

No line number beyond the one it sits on. No "because". No "try this instead". Just the three words, and a name beside them I recognise from the team list, and a little grey timestamp that says it arrived at 08:47, twenty-five minutes before I got to my desk.

I read it again. Then I read it a third time, slower, as if the extra words might be hiding between the three that are there. They are not.

The line it sits on is mine. It sorts a list of invoices by date, and I wrote it on Tuesday afternoon, in a hurry, because the dashboard needed it and the afternoon was already gone. I remember writing it. I remember feeling clever about it for about four seconds, which is the usual length of time I feel clever about anything I write.

09:14. I click on the file. The function is eleven lines long. I read it the way you read a text from someone you like, looking for the tone underneath the words. It sorts. It returns. It handles the empty list. I check the tests. Two tests, both green, both mine. I run them again anyway, because running them feels like doing something, and they go green again, which tells me nothing except that the tests agree with me, and the tests were written by me, so of course they agree with me.

09:31. I start a reply.

"Could you say a bit more about what's wrong here? Happy to fix it."

I read it back. It sounds fine. It sounds like a person who is not bothered at all. I delete it. It sounds too fine, which is the problem. If I send that, I will spend the rest of the day wondering whether she thinks I am being passive-aggressive, and she will spend the rest of the day wondering whether I am. Nobody wins.

09:47. Second draft.

"Which part is wrong? The sort, or the date handling?"

Shorter. Honest. I hover over the button. My finger does not press it. Because what if she answers "both", and then I have to ask again, and now I am the person who needs three rounds of comments to understand one line of code. I delete it too.

10:05. Third draft, and this one is long. It explains why I wrote it this way. It mentions the Tuesday deadline. It points out that the tests pass. It has a paragraph about the date format coming in as a string from the old system, which is true, and which has nothing to do with anything. I read the whole thing and I can hear how it sounds: a man building a small fort out of excuses and sitting inside it. I select all of it and delete it, and the empty box looks back at me, and I feel better and worse at the same time.

10:40. I give up on the reply and go back to the code. This is the part of the day where I become a detective in my own flat, looking for something I lost in a room I cleaned myself.

Maybe it is the sort. The dates arrive as strings, "2026-11-04", "2026-11-19", and string sort works fine on those, until it doesn't. I think about it. It works fine. I think about it more. It still works fine. I think about it until "works fine" starts to sound like something a person says right before finding out it doesn't.

Maybe it is the empty list. Maybe it is the duplicate dates. Maybe it is the fact that I named the variable sorted and shadowed something somewhere. I open the file that calls this function. I open the file that calls that file. By 11:20 I have five tabs open and I am reading code I wrote last month as if it were written by a stranger who might have left me a clue.

11:58. I close the tabs. I have found three things that might be wrong, and I am not sure about any of them, and the honest truth is that I could rewrite the whole function in twenty minutes and still not know whether I fixed the thing she meant. I eat lunch at my desk, which I never do, because leaving the desk feels like leaving the argument, and the argument is only happening in my head, and I cannot leave my head.

13:20. I check the thread. Nothing new. The three words are still there, patient as a parked car. I read them again and this time I notice the full stop. "This is wrong." The full stop makes it worse. Without it, it could be a thought she typed quickly. With it, it sounds finished. Settled. A verdict with nowhere to go.

13:44. I open the reply box again. I type "Thanks for catching this —" and stop. Thanks for catching what? I do not know what she caught. I am thanking her for a mystery. I delete it.

14:15. I do actual work for an hour, or I pretend to. I fix a typo in a readme. I rename a variable in a file nobody will ever open. I answer two messages with unusual speed, because answering messages is a thing I can complete, and the comment is a thing I cannot. Every ten minutes I click back to the pull request, the way you check a phone that has not buzzed, and every time the thread is the same, and every time I am a little annoyed at myself for checking.

15:30. I write the reply I should have written at 09:14. Six words.

"What part is wrong? Happy to fix."

No explanation, no defence, no "thanks for catching this". Just the question, asked plainly, the way I would ask it if she were sitting next to me and I had not spent six hours making it complicated. I press the button before I can re-read it. The page reloads. My question sits under her comment, small and a little bit naked, and there is nothing to do now except wait, which turns out to be its own kind of work.

16:02. She is online. I can see the little dot. I watch the dot the way you watch a kettle. The dot stays. Nothing arrives. I open another file and stare at it without reading it.

16:41. The reply comes. Two lines.

"The sort compares the strings, so the 9th sorts after the 19th. Compare the timestamps instead."

I read it twice. Then I laugh, out loud, alone, at my desk, because of course. Of course it is the dates. The strings sort fine until the day number hits double digits and then "9" sits after "19" like it owns the place, and every invoice from the first nine days of the month has been sitting in the wrong order for a week, and the tests passed because both my test dates were in the twenties. A four-minute fix. A four-minute fix that cost me a Thursday.

16:47. I change one line. I compare the timestamps. I run the tests. Green. I add a third test with a date on the 9th and a date on the 19th, because that is the test I should have written on Tuesday, and it goes red before the fix and green after, which is the sound a test is supposed to make. I push. I write "Fixed — sorting by timestamp now, added a test for single-digit days." I press the button. The thread closes itself in my head the way a door closes when you finally stop holding it open.

17:20. The rest of the day is quiet. The quiet is the strange part. The comment is answered, the code is fixed, and there is nothing left to be angry about, which leaves me with the anger and nowhere to put it. I keep thinking about the six hours. Not the bug. The bug was four minutes. The six hours were mine. I spent them writing replies I never sent and reading code I had already read, because three words with no "because" felt like a verdict, and I treated it like one, and a verdict is something you defend yourself against, and a question is something you just answer.

18:35. A pull request from someone else lands in my queue. A new joiner, three weeks in, and I open it, and I read it, and I find the thing that is wrong. It is a small thing. A loop that runs one time too many. I click on the line. The comment box opens, empty and patient. I type "this is wrong" and I look at it, sitting there in the box, three words and a full stop, and I delete it.

I write the other version instead. The line number, and what it does wrong, and what to change, and the two minutes it will take. I read it back and it sounds like a person who wants the code fixed, not a person who wants to be right. I press the button. The comment goes out with my name beside it, and the thread waits, and somewhere on the other side of it a person is about to have a much shorter Thursday than I did.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: My --config-test accepted a listen address that could never bind
articles.description: transponder is a Go proxy I've been building. It has a --config-test flag: load the config, validate...
articles.body_html:
transponder is a Go proxy I've been building. It has a --config-test flag: load the config, validate it, exit 0 or 1. It runs in CI and in the deploy script before anything starts.

Last week a config passed --config-test and the server died 200 ms later with:

listen tcp: lookup tcp/nope: unknown port

No key name, no line number, nothing to grep for. The config had listen_addr: ":nope".

The check I wrote

Validation did the obvious thing: net.SplitHostPort, then strconv.Atoi and a range check. It felt correct because the standard library was doing the parsing.

SplitHostPort is a splitter, not a validator. Here it is against the values that kill net.Listen (Go 1.27.1, on this box):

SplitHostPort(":")             = "",          "",      <nil>
SplitHostPort(":nope")         = "",          "nope",  <nil>
SplitHostPort(":70000")        = "",          "70000", <nil>
SplitHostPort("localhost:+80") = "localhost", "+80",   <nil>

Every one splits fine. net.Listen disagrees with some of them:

:nope    -> listen tcp: lookup tcp/nope: unknown port
:70000   -> listen tcp: address 70000: invalid port
:        -> ok on [::]:39331
:+0      -> ok on [::]:44017

: — the value that looks most broken — binds a free port quite happily. And :+0 binds too: signed ports are legal, which I had assumed they weren't. So the port has to be read the way net.Listen reads it — a number in 0–65535, or a service name resolved through net.LookupPort — and not with whatever cut the string.

func splitListenAddr(key, addr string) (host string, port int, err error) {
    rawHost, rawPort, err := net.SplitHostPort(addr)
    if err != nil || rawPort == "" {
        return "", 0, fmt.Errorf("config: %s %q must be host:port, such as :8080", key, addr)
    }
    if n, err := strconv.Atoi(rawPort); err == nil {
        if n < 0 || n > 65535 {
            return "", 0, fmt.Errorf("config: %s %q has the port %q, which must be between 0 and 65535", key, addr, rawPort)
        }
        return rawHost, n, nil
    }
    n, err := net.LookupPort("tcp", rawPort)
    if err != nil {
        return "", 0, fmt.Errorf("config: %s %q names the port %q, which is neither a number nor a known service", key, addr, rawPort)
    }
    return rawHost, n, nil
}

No socket opened, no DNS. LookupPort reads the local service list, which is the same list net.Listen would read.

Then the two-listener case

The service has a main listener and an ops listener. The same port on both is a startup failure, so the config check compares them — except when either port is 0, which asks the kernel for a free one.

Comparing hosts is net.IP.Equal plus case folding, with a zone split off first because net.ParseIP doesn't read zones. Fine. Then I wrote the wildcard rule: an unspecified address reaches everything, so refuse it next to any host on the same port.

CodeRabbit said I had that backwards for 0.0.0.0 next to [::1]. I said no — they bind separately, the v4 wildcard is v4.

They were right, and it took one command:

$ go run .   # listen on 0.0.0.0:42771, then [::1]:42771
[::1]:42771 -> listen tcp [::1]:42771: bind: address already in use

Go's favoriteAddrFamily opens an IPv4 wildcard as a dual-stack AF_INET6 socket, so 0.0.0.0 claims the v6 side as well. ss -lnt6 lists it, ss -lnt4 doesn't. My mental model came from C, not from net/ipsock_posix.go.

What shipped is the conservative rule: any unspecified host conflicts with anything on that port. On a platform that binds the v4 wildcard v4-only, that refuses a pair which would have worked — and a config that passes and then can't start is exactly the bug the check exists to catch.

Zones are the same story

net.ParseIP ignores zones, so fe80::1%eth0 and fe80::1%eth1 compare equal and a real collision between two interfaces slips through. Split on the first %, compare address and zone separately, and refuse what net.Listen refuses:

127.0.0.1%lo:0      -> lookup 127.0.0.1%lo: no such host   (v4 takes no zone)
[fe80::1%]:0        -> lookup fe80::1%: no such host       (empty zone)
[fe80::1%eth0%x]:0  -> bind: invalid argument              (second %)

The rule

A config check earns its keep only if it reads each value the way the consumer reads it. Same parser, same edge cases, same refusals — or explicit, documented strictness where reproducing the consumer is impossible. Anything else is a linter wearing a --config-test sticker: it approves the file, the process dies anyway, and the error arrives without the key that caused it.

Eighty lines and two test tables to move one class of startup failure from 11pm to CI. Worth it. The patch is #206 on raven-clown/transponder if you want to read the reject cases.

articles.title: Meet BetterZoom: the only self diagnostic app with smart rowdy intelligence needed
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge             What I Built   For...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge
 

What I Built

For the SmartSpectra SDK Challenge, I built an app that might make Zoom, google meet obsolete forever considering the office meetings are highly unproductive due to managers fail to keep tabs on their juniors/team members & ultimately failing to track their emotional/mental state; results in dead productivity. My app features 2 modes: self mode which is uniquly built to train/regulate your ownself for tough situations. The next feature is main highlight (Meetings) which would allow a host to combine the power of SDK monitoring with use Artifical Intelligence to be much more aware about their team mates.

Meeting Mode (main highlight)

The problem

  • Meetings eat up a huge share of the working day, and most people think they don't work. In a Harvard Business School survey of 182 senior managers, 71% said meetings are unproductive and inefficient, and 65% said meetings keep them from finishing their own work.
  • In Atlassian's 2024 State of Teams survey of 5,000 knowledge workers, 78% said they struggle to get their work done because of how many meetings they have.
  • A big reason: the host can't watch everyone at once. With 5 other faces on screen, it's easy to miss who has switched off, who is nervous to speak, or who is overwhelmed. The meeting slowly loses its purpose.

What BetterZoom does about it

  • Every participant who agrees is measured on their own laptop: pulse, breathing, HRV and face signals (looking at the screen, talking, blinking, expressions).
  • The host sees a live one-word state next to each person's video, updated every second: Calm, Steady, Tense or Anxious. No charts, no clutter, unless the host wants them.
  • Every 25 seconds, a small summary of numbers (never video) goes to the host. It covers attention, talking time, expressions and heart rhythm.
  • The host taps the bot on someone's card, and Smokey writes a 3–4 line summary in seconds: how that person seems now, what changed over the meeting, and a gentle suggestion like "invite their thoughts" or "give them a moment." He can read it out loud.
  • One tap for the full picture: a report window with trend charts for pulse, breathing and HRV, attention signals and expressions.
  • Before leaving, the host can download a .md report card for every participant, or a CSV of all readings.

Built on consent, not surveillance

  • Nobody is measured unless they say yes. Everyone sees a "Reporting to host" badge on anyone who is sharing, and anyone can stop with one click.
  • The AI only ever sees "P1, P2…", never names or video. Everything is wiped when the host leaves the meeting.

In numbers: up to 6 people per meeting · live state every 1 s · reports every 25 s · AI summary on demand in 3–4 lines · 0 videos uploaded or stored.

Self Mode

  • Built for emotional and mental regulation for tense situation preparation: Job interviews, Public speaking, or Startup Pitches. Even managers can use this feature to prep before hoping on a call or briefing about something important to their bosses.

  • Monitors your facial expression, registers your emotional state and uses Smart Intelligence system (Smokey Bot referrence in the video) to help you navigate through the situation.

  • Smokey turns your signals into coaching. Every 30 seconds he gets a snapshot of your pulse, breathing rate, HRV, calm level and expressions, compared with your own normal. He also knows what you're practising for.

  • He reads the patterns. Fast breathing and a rising pulse usually mean nerves, which is common in a job interview. He spots that and gives you a quick fix, like "inhale for four seconds, exhale for six" or "drop your shoulders and pause before answering." Calm numbers? He tells you to keep that pace.

  • A real example: in one of my runs my breathing jumped to about 30 breaths a minute while I talked. Smokey caught it within half a minute and walked me through slowing it down.

 

Demo


 

Code

Github Repo: https://github.com/Msohaib-maker/SneakMeet

Note: My Github repo includes all the necessary intructions to install & use the Windows App.

How It Responds to Human Signals

We have SDK integrated in both of our app modules: self mode and Group Mode. The SDK provides us the following readings:

Reading What it means
Pulse Compared with your own resting pulse, not an average person's. "↑ a bit higher than usual" means something.
Breathing rate The strongest sign of nerves in my testing. Fast breathing pushes the calm meter towards Tense.
HRV (plus average beat gap, SDNN and stress index) Shown once you've sat still for about a minute. Higher variability usually means more relaxed.
Breathing waveforms (chest and belly) Drawn live, and used to tell whether you breathe mostly from your chest or your belly.
Pulse waveform Drawn live, one peak per heartbeat.
Expressions, blinking, talking Your main expression appears as a meme-style sticker on your video. Talking tells the app to ignore breathing for a moment, because speech throws breathing readings off.

How the experience reacts in real time

Self mode (practising for an interview, pitch or talk):

  1. For the first ~30 seconds the app quietly learns your normal pulse and breathing.
  2. After that, a calm meter (Calm → Steady → Tense → Anxious) moves as your body reacts, with the reason shown underneath: "Pulse 86, 8 above your baseline."
  3. Every 30 seconds the numbers go to Gemini, and Smokey (my AI host) answers in character and out loud. In one of my runs my breathing climbed to around 30 breaths a minute while I talked. Smokey noticed and told me: "Slow your breathing right down by inhaling for four seconds and exhaling for six."
  4. At the end you get a debrief: how your calm level changed over the session, strengths, things to work on, and a downloadable report.

Meeting mode:

  1. Participants who agree to share get a live one-word state next to their video: Calm, Steady, Tense or Anxious. Only the host sees it.
  2. Every 25 seconds a small summary (numbers only) goes to the host.
  3. The host taps the little bot on someone's card, and Gemini writes a 3–4 line summary of how that person seems and what changed. Smokey can read it out.

How I integrated the SDK

  • BetterZoom is an Electron desktop app using @smartspectra/node-sdk. The same camera stream feeds both the video call and the SDK (useMediaStream), so nobody needs two cameras.
  • I request three groups of readings: breathing (rate plus chest/belly traces), heart (pulse, pressure waveform, HRV) and face (blinks, talking, expressions). The SDK sends roughly 28 updates a second, which I decode with decodeMetrics.
  • I only trust readings the SDK is confident about: below 45% for pulse or 40% for breathing, the app shows the number faded with a "weak signal" label instead of guessing.
  • The SDK's camera checks (face too low, chest not visible, frame rate too low) appear on screen as plain tips, so people can fix their setup themselves.
  • The calm meter is my own logic on top of the SDK. It compares pulse and breathing with your personal baseline, smooths them out, and ignores breathing while you talk.

My honest experience

After about 90 credits of testing:

  • Expressions and breathing came through well. Most of the time the SDK reported around 68–73% confidence for me, and the readings matched how I actually felt.
  • Pulse usually appears after 15–25 seconds. I'm not a medical expert, so I can't judge how accurate it is, but it stayed in a believable range and reacted when I got nervous.
  • Expressions are not perfect. The SDK sometimes read me as neutral or sad when I was actually tense.
  • Breathing needs your chest in view, and HRV needs about a minute of sitting still. That's rare while you're talking, so HRV often didn't show up during practice.
  • Frame rate is the big one. The SDK needs 25+ fps and stops itself if the camera can't keep up. At first my app was the problem: redrawing the screen on every update and animating Smokey starved the SDK, and it stopped after about 15 seconds. Throttling the UI, freezing animations while measuring, and sending lighter video in meetings took my runs from stopping early to 5 minutes without a break. Dim rooms and power-saving laptops can still cause it, because webcams lower their frame rate in bad light.
  • Some readings listed in the SDK (breathing amplitude, apnea, inhale/exhale ratio) aren't available yet. Requesting them makes the SDK refuse to start, so I left them out.

The 68–73% figure and the expression observations are yours, so I've kept them as your experience. Everything else comes from the logs of our test runs.

Prize Categories

I am going to say I would personally put my app in Thoughful Category with a bit of creativity. Office meetings as I mentioned earlier woul have been the best use case for my application given the API has high amount of credits. Given SDK can be used to monitor particpants' expressions and state of comfort would help the team managers/HRs to be better decision makers. We might be looking forward to see many people never mad to be part of meetings because of their state of comfort or we could be looking to companies adapting to new meet policies which ultimately get them better meet profits.

Consent and Data Handling

Camera consent

  • BetterZoom only uses your camera and microphone after Windows asks for your permission. No other page or website can use them.
  • Readings are off until you start them yourself: by pressing Practice solo, Measure vitals or Start scan.
  • In meetings, nothing is shared by default. When a meeting has a host, every participant sees a consent popup first. It names the host and explains what will be measured, what is sent, how often, and that an AI may summarise it. You can say no and still stay in the meeting.
  • While someone is sharing, everyone in the meeting sees a "Reporting to host" badge on their video. They can stop at any time with one click. There is no hidden or background monitoring.

What is measured and where it goes

  • All readings (pulse, breathing, HRV, waveforms, face signals and expressions) are calculated on your own computer by the SmartSpectra SDK. Video frames are never uploaded or recorded.
  • Self mode: your readings stay on your laptop. Only numbers go to the AI (see below).
  • Meetings: video and audio go directly between participants (peer-to-peer, encrypted by WebRTC). A participant's readings go only to the host, and only if they agreed: a short update every second, plus a summary every 25 seconds. These are numbers only, never images.
  • Our server (on Fly.io) helps people connect and passes AI requests on to Gemini. It never sees video and stores nothing.

AI (Google Gemini)

  • Smokey's coaching and summaries are written by Google Gemini. The app sends only numbers (pulse, breathing, calm level, expression scores), never video.
  • In meetings, participants are sent as P1, P2…, never by name. The real name is added back on the host's computer.
  • On Gemini's free tier, Google may use this data to improve its products. The consent popup says so.
  • Smokey's voice uses the voices built into Windows, which work offline. No audio is sent anywhere.

Storage, retention and deletion

  • Nothing is stored on a server. In meetings, reports and AI summaries live only in the host's app memory and are deleted when the host leaves the meeting or closes the app.
  • Files (the Self mode debrief, report cards, CSV) are saved only if you click download. They are then your files to keep or delete.
  • The app keeps only your settings on your computer. Uninstalling the app removes them.

SDK telemetry

  • The SmartSpectra SDK signs in to Presage with an API key, which lives on our server and is handed to the app when measuring starts. It also sends session telemetry by default; see Presage's Telemetry and Privacy (https://smartspectra.presagetech.com/docs/telemetry-and-privacy) page.

Not medical

  • All values are wellness estimates. BetterZoom is not a medical device, makes no diagnosis, and must not be used for medical decisions. Labels like "Calm" or "Tense" are estimates from camera readings, not facts about how someone feels.
