articles.title: Interaction Nets Explained: The Programming Model Behind the Frostbite CPU
articles.description: On November 18, 2026, the chip-design startup Architect Labs published a post introducing Frostbite....
articles.body_html:
On November 18, 2026, the chip-design startup Architect Labs published a post introducing Frostbite. They describe it as a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set. They say their AI systems designed it, from the compiler down to the final chip layout. The Hacker News thread reached 657 points and 342 comments.

Most coverage is about the AI and the headline number: 4.59x better performance per watt than a conventional core. This article looks at the part software developers can try today. Frostbite runs programs as interaction nets, a model of computation that is more than 35 years old. The language that compiles to it, Vine, is open source, and you can install it with Cargo today.

A note on sources: I have not run Vine or seen Frostbite hardware. Every number below comes from the linked sources: the Frostbite post, the Vine documentation, an explainer from the company behind Vine, and the HN discussion.

What Frostbite claims, in short

All of these come from the Architect Labs post:

  • The workloads. 25 programs in five groups: parallel, staged, sequential, branching, and recursive. The agents tuned the design on 10 of them. The other 15 were held out until the final evaluation.
  • The headline result. One Frostbite "quad" (a two-by-two group of tiles) reached a geometric mean of 4.59x the performance per watt of the comparison core across all 25 workloads. That splits into 6.02x on the 10 tuning workloads and 3.83x on the 15 held-out ones.
  • Area. An average 8.77x performance per area, on a 7 nm process.
  • The baseline. The comparison core is "a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core". A footnote says: "For legal reasons, we cannot disclose the exact CPU."
  • The status. The design reached 500 MHz in the final GDS (the layout file sent to a chip factory). The post itself calls the power numbers "pre-silicon". It does not report results from a manufactured chip.
  • The process. The specification ended as formal contracts that compiled to more than 800,000 lines of Lean (a proof assistant). The agents tried 58 design ideas and kept 37.

Why can this design drop so much of a normal CPU's hardware? The answer is in the programming model.

Why your CPU spends energy guessing

A normal compiler sees which operations in your program depend on each other. It uses that information for optimization. Then it throws most of it away and produces one long list of instructions.

The CPU then tries to rebuild that information at runtime. Out-of-order cores keep large buffers to find instructions that can run early. Multicore chips add cache coherence protocols so every core sees the same memory, because any instruction might touch any address.

The explainer from Tendrils, the company that develops Vine, puts it this way: "Normal compilers already track these dependencies internally and use them to make optimizations. However, this information is then thrown away and the entire program is linearized into a sequence of instructions."

Frostbite's post shows the cost. Leaving out clock distribution, the comparison core spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Only 13% goes to computing. Interaction nets keep the dependency information instead.

Interaction nets in four ideas

Interaction nets were introduced by Yves Lafont in a 1990 paper at POPL, a major programming-languages conference. The model fits in four ideas.

1. A program is a graph of nodes. Each node has exactly one principal port (its main connection point) and zero or more auxiliary ports (extra connection points). Wires connect ports. In the simple examples, a number and an addition are both nodes.

2. Computation is rewriting pairs. When a wire connects the principal ports of two nodes, they form an active pair. A rule says how that pair is replaced by a small new piece of graph. Then the next active pair is rewritten, and so on, until none are left. Each step only touches the two nodes involved. Tendrils calls this property locality.

3. Active pairs never overlap. A node has only one principal port, so it can be part of only one active pair at a time. That means all active pairs are independent. You can rewrite them in any order, or all at once, and the final result is the same. This property is called confluence. In practice it means no race conditions: there is no shared variable for two threads to fight over.

4. Every value is used exactly once. This is linearity. If a value needs to be used twice, the net contains an explicit duplicate node. If it is not used, an explicit erase node destroys it. Nothing is copied or dropped by accident. Rust developers will recognize the idea: it is close to ownership.

The Tendrils explainer shows this with unary arithmetic. In its multiplication example, the first rewrite leaves two independent active pairs, which can run in parallel with no coordination. Nobody added that parallelism. It is a side effect of keeping the dependencies.

What linearity looks like in Vine

Nobody wants to wire graph nodes by hand. Vine is a language with syntax close to Rust that compiles to interaction nets. Its Apache-2.0 GitHub repository calls it "an experimental new programming language based on interaction nets". Vine compiles to Ivy, a low-level net language, which runs on a runtime called the IVM. The Frostbite post says programs for the chip are written in Vine and compiled to Ivy.

Linearity shows up in Vine's type system as "flexibility". The Fork and Drop documentation says every type has two yes-or-no properties: can its values be forked (copied), and can they be dropped (destroyed)? The annotations work like regex quantifiers:

  • No annotation: values must be used exactly once.
  • ?: values may be used zero or one times (droppable).
  • +: values may be used one or more times (forkable).
  • *: values may be used zero or more times (both).

When you use a variable twice, the compiler inserts a fork for you. The docs show (used_multiple_times, used_multiple_times) becoming (used_multiple_times.fork(), used_multiple_times) behind the scenes.

The IO type cannot be forked or dropped. The docs explain the result: "at any point in the execution of a Vine program, there is exactly one IO handle, so all IO operations are ordered." So the language gets ordered side effects from the type system, while pure computation stays free to run in parallel.

Measure your program's parallelism with one flag

Vine can tell you how parallel a program is, without any parallel hardware.

The installation page needs Rust and one command:

cargo install --git https://github.com/VineLang/vine --locked

Every Vine program needs a main function that takes the IO handle. The hello world is:

pub fn main(&io: &IO) {
  io.println("Hello, world!");
}

Run it with vine run hello_world.vi. After the output, Vine prints statistics. The docs show 341 total interactions for this program. The statistics page says the total interaction count is deterministic: "the same program will always have the exact same interaction count, no matter what machine it is run on." That makes it a stable measure of work, unlike wall-clock time.

The useful flag is --breadth-first. The CLI docs say it runs the program so that "at each step, every possible interaction is performed in parallel." This pretends you have a machine with unlimited cores. It reports three numbers:

  • Total: all interactions, the amount of work.
  • Depth: the number of parallel steps needed. This is the critical path, the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another.
  • Breadth: total divided by depth, the average number of interactions ready at each step.

This is the work-span model from algorithms courses: total is the work, depth is the span, and breadth is the average parallelism.

A worked example: longest common subsequence

The Tendrils explainer uses the longest common subsequence problem. Given two lists, find the length of the longest sequence of items that appears in both, in order, but not always next to each other. For "Tendrils" and "edits", the answer is "edis", length 4.

Here is their Vine code, a plain dynamic-programming version with two nested loops and no parallel hints:

pub fn lcs[T*; Eq[T]](a: List[T], b: List[T]) -> N32 {
  let row = [];
  for a_elem in a {
    let prev_row_entry = 0;
    let prev_new_entry = 0;
    let new_row = [];
    for b_elem in b {
      let row_entry = row.pop_front().or_use(0);
      let new_entry = if a_elem == b_elem {
        prev_row_entry + 1
      } else {
        row_entry.max(prev_new_entry)
      };
      prev_row_entry = row_entry;
      prev_new_entry = new_entry;
      new_row.push_back(new_entry);
    }
    row = new_row;
  }

  row.get(b.len() - 1).or_use(0)
}

Note the T* in the signature. With the flexibility rules above, that says list items may be copied or dropped freely.

They ran it on two random lists of 200 items with vine run lcs.vi --breadth-first:

Interactions
  Total            2_993_893
    Depth             10_920
    Breadth              274

On average, 274 interactions could run at each step. Then they increased both lists to 2,000 items:

Interactions
  Total          296_223_905
    Depth            108_142
    Breadth            2_739

The total work grew about 100x, because the algorithm is quadratic. The depth grew only about 10x. The explainer gives the reason: every cell on a diagonal of the DP table is independent of the others, so the critical path is just the main diagonal, which grows linearly. The parallel work grows with the input.

The explainer says the Vine compiler does this "not by magically extracting parallelism out of the program; it simply preserves dependency information all the way down to the hardware (or runtime, in this case)."

Frostbite's post shows the same pattern on a smaller problem. For five queens on a five-by-five board, the net runs 3,183 interactions with a critical path of 262 steps. On average, about twelve interactions are ready at every step.

How to read your own numbers

If you try this on your own algorithms, keep two limits in mind:

  • Breadth-first mode is optimistic. The CLI docs say it "gives an upper bound on the speedup that could be seen from a parallel machine." Real hardware has a fixed number of cores and pays to move work between them.
  • Depth is the floor. No hardware can finish faster than the critical path. A program with a breadth near 1 is sequential, whatever the chip is. This is close to Amdahl's law, and one HN commenter made that point about general-purpose code: "the longest serial task is what ends up slowing everything down."

From a net to a chip: how Frostbite schedules work

Frostbite is a grid of tiles. Each tile has a small local memory, an engine, and a runtime block. Because every value has one owner and every step is local, data can sit in small memories next to where it is used, instead of in a deep shared cache.

There is no central scheduler. The Frostbite post says each tile follows three rules:

  1. Run your own work first (the work in your input ports).
  2. If you have none, take work from a neighboring tile that has some to spare.
  3. If no neighbor has any, go inactive and save power.

Per the post, when a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces, the running code parks what comes next in a small record (the "frame manager"), puts the new tasks on a hardware "work queue", and takes the newest one itself. Idle neighbors pull the rest over the on-chip network. When the last piece returns, the parked code wakes up.

The post calls this "stealing work". Java developers know the same idea from ForkJoinPool, which its docs describe as "employing work-stealing". Here it is built into the tile hardware. The post says no human specified it and that it can be traced to "necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics."

The energy breakdown shows the trade. A Frostbite quad cuts memory energy to 38% and fetch, decode, and issue to 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on the on-chip network and scheduler. Frostbite moves energy from guessing about dependencies to moving messages between tiles.

What the numbers do not show yet

The baseline is a small core, and it is not named. A dual-issue, in-order core is far simpler than the out-of-order cores in laptops and servers. One HN commenter pointed this out: "Actual modern high-performance CPUs use way larger than dual-issue front-ends." The post says comparisons against larger out-of-order CPUs, multicore setups, and the SPEC and PARSEC benchmark suites are planned "in the coming months".

The power numbers are pre-silicon. They come from models and RTL (hardware description code), not a measured chip. The post says they can be matched to real chips "over multiple tapeout loops", which has not happened yet.

The held-out score is the one to quote. The post reports both 6.02x on tuning workloads and 3.83x on held-out ones. When someone repeats "4.59x", remember that 3.83x is the number for programs the design never saw.

The workloads are small. Three kernels follow the SPLASH-2 suite but are "64 times smaller", per the post. Another HN commenter noted that the tests are compute-heavy kernels on small working sets, and asked how the design handles programs that "build large data structures and slowly mutate them."

Debugging changes. A commenter pointed out that there is no call stack or program counter, and that nets can leak values or get stuck waiting on each other. Vine's own statistics page touches on this: the Allocated and Freed memory numbers should always match, and "if they differ, that indicates that there was a vicious circle in the interaction net." Vine has a debug mode, but the same commenter called a source-level debugger "a requirement" and said that building one, if it does not exist yet, "would represent a substantial engineering project."

Some framing is disputed. The Frostbite post and the Tendrils explainer both say single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s; one commenter disagreed, citing yearly gains in Apple's chips. Another argued that the ideas came from decades of human research, and the AI turned them into an engineered product.

Who builds what

Two companies appear in this story. Architect Labs built Frostbite; its launch post mentions "$24M in seed funding led by Kindred Ventures". Tendrils develops Vine; its November 10 announcement says it raised $30M in a round led by Benchmark to build its own processor "to have thousands of cores operating in parallel."

The Frostbite post cites Vine and the Tendrils explainer. An HN commenter asked whether the two companies are related. Neither post says, so treat them as separate projects that share a language.

The Frostbite post lists its next steps: an FPGA-hosted playground where anyone can run programs, a basic operating system, benchmarks against a broader set of CPUs, and a release of the RTL and ISA.

What you can do with this today

  • Run your algorithms with --breadth-first. Depth and breadth show how much of your code is a serial chain and how much is independent work. If a rewrite lowers depth, it has more room for parallel speedup on any machine.
  • Notice where you share mutable state. Interaction nets make every copy and drop explicit. Asking "who owns this value?" in Java, Go, or Rust is the same habit that makes concurrent code safer.
  • Watch for the FPGA playground and the SPEC results. They will show whether the 3.83x held-out number survives real hardware and stronger baselines.

Frostbite may or may not become a product. The model under it is well defined and available now in a language you can install with one command.

Would you write code for a chip with no program counter and no shared memory, if the tooling caught leaks and stuck nets for you?

Sources

  • [1] Introducing Frostbite, Architect Labs
  • [2] Hacker News discussion of Frostbite
  • [3] On Interaction Nets, Tendrils
  • [4] Interaction nets, Wikipedia (cites Lafont, POPL 1990)
  • [5] Vine documentation
  • [6] Vine on GitHub
  • [7] Vine docs: Fork and Drop
  • [8] Vine docs: Using the CLI
  • [9] Vine docs: Statistics
  • [10] Introducing Architect Labs
  • [11] Tendrils: $30M Raised to Redo the CPU

articles.title: I built a background remover that runs 100% in the browser. Here's how I made it 7x faster
articles.description: Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you...
articles.body_html:
Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you to pay for the full-resolution download. I wanted the opposite: the photo never leaves your device, the download is full resolution, and there is no account.

So I built Remove de Fundo, a background remover where the AI model runs entirely in the browser. The first version worked, but on real phones it was slow enough that people left before seeing a result. This post is about what made it slow and what fixed it.

End result on the same laptop and the same photo: 43.8 s → 6.4 s from click to cutout.

The stack

  • Astro for the site (static pages, deployed to Cloudflare Workers)
  • @imgly/background-removal with the IS-Net fp16 model (~88 MB)
  • ONNX Runtime Web, which runs the model with WebGPU on desktop and WebAssembly (CPU) on phones
  • A small post-processing step in canvas to clean up semi-transparent "haze" in the mask

Everything happens client-side. The server only serves static files.

Problem 1: the model came from a CDN that didn't cache

The first visit downloads ~100 MB (model + ONNX runtime). That is unavoidable for an in-browser model, but I noticed something worse: the CDN serving the model sent no Cache-Control header, and the edge marked it cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC. So returning visitors were often downloading the model again, and nothing was cached near the user.

Fix: self-host the model files. A build script downloads the model chunks once and puts them in public/ai/<version>/, and the library is pointed there with publicPath. Since the chunk file names are content hashes, they can be cached forever:

/ai/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Now a returning visitor loads the model from disk cache: zero network.

One gotcha: the chunk files have no extension, and both the dev server and the host treated extensionless paths as pages (404). Saving them as <hash>.bin and rewriting the names in resources.json fixed it.

Problem 2: the CPU path used one core out of eight

Phones always use the WebAssembly path, so CPU speed matters most. ONNX Runtime Web can use multiple threads, but only if the page is cross-origin isolated, because threads need SharedArrayBuffer.

My page wasn't isolated:

crossOriginIsolated // false

Fix: two headers.

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless

I used credentialless instead of require-corp so Google Fonts and analytics keep working without CORP headers. Browsers that don't support it simply ignore it, so nothing breaks there.

Result (CPU, model already loaded): 22.7 s → 7.9 s per photo. Almost 3x, from two lines of config.

Problem 3: the bug that made PNG encoding 13x slower

After enabling isolation, inference got much faster but the total barely improved. I logged a timestamp for each stage and found this:

Stage Time
Inference 1.5 s
PNG encode 5.5 s
Edge refinement 4.4 s

Encoding a 1200 × 800 PNG should take a fraction of a second. I measured canvas.convertToBlob() on an idle page:

Page PNG encode
Not isolated 208 ms
Isolated, before loading ONNX 217 ms
Isolated, after running ONNX 2,648 ms

So isolation itself was fine. The problem: the library sets the WASM thread count to navigator.hardwareConcurrency (all cores), and ONNX's worker threads keep spin-waiting after inference. They occupy every core, and the browser's own image-encoding threads starve.

Fix: cap the thread count before the library loads. I used ONNX Runtime's own default (half the cores, at most 4) on CPU, and 1 thread on the GPU path, where the GPU does the work:

function limitOnnxThreads(device: 'gpu' | 'cpu') {
  const cores = navigator.hardwareConcurrency || 4;
  const threads = device === 'gpu' ? 1 : Math.max(1, Math.min(4, Math.ceil(cores / 2)));
  Object.defineProperty(navigator, 'hardwareConcurrency', {
    configurable: true,
    get: () => threads,
  });
}

Post-processing went from ~10 s back to 0.2 s.

Problem 4: the first photo on WebGPU paid for shader compilation

On the WebGPU path, the second photo took 2 s but the first took ~17 s on every page load. The session creation and, mostly, the first inference compile the GPU shaders.

Fix: warm up on intent. When the user hovers the upload area (desktop) or taps it (mobile), I:

  1. Prefetch the model files into the HTTP cache (low priority).
  2. Call the library's preload() with exactly the same config as the real run (the library memoizes the session by JSON.stringify(config)).
  3. On GPU only, run one throwaway inference on a tiny 32×32 image. The model input has a fixed size, so this compiles everything the real photo needs.

While the person is still picking a photo from their gallery, all of that is already happening. I skip the warm inference on CPU: on a phone it would take as long as a real cutout and the user's photo would wait behind it. I also skip prefetching on saveData or 2G connections, and on mobile only a tap on the upload box triggers it, so scrolling past doesn't burn 100 MB of someone's data.

Things I tried that didn't work

  • The smaller quantized model (isnet_quint8, 44 MB). Half the download, but it left patches of background all over a portrait. Not worth it.
  • Relying on HTTP heuristic caching for a third-party CDN. In practice, returning visitors still re-downloaded.

UX fixes that mattered as much as speed

  • The upload box was below the fold on a 730 px laptop screen. People saw a headline and left. Tightening the hero put the button in the first screen on laptops and phones.
  • Show the user's own photo with a scanning line while processing, instead of a generic spinner. It makes the wait feel much shorter.
  • On mobile, the label "Drag your photo here" makes no sense. It now says "Choose a photo".

Results

Before After
Click → result (laptop, first run) 43.8 s 6.4 s
CPU inference per photo 22.7 s 7.9 s
PNG encode + edge cleanup ~10 s (isolated, before fix) 0.2 s
Returning visitor model download often ~100 MB 0 (disk cache)

Since adding analytics, about 98% of removals succeed and more than half of the people who upload a photo download the result.

Credits

The heavy lifting is done by IMG.LY's background-removal-js (AGPL-3.0) and ONNX Runtime Web. If you build something similar, check their licenses.

You can try it here: removedefundo.com/en. It's free, with no sign-up, and works in English, Spanish and Portuguese. I'd love feedback, especially from people on older phones.

This post was written with AI assistance. The numbers come from real measurements on the live site.

articles.title: I built a CLI that turns any place on Earth into a pixel-art diorama
articles.description: Type a place, get an isometric pixel-art poster, video or GIF built from OpenStreetMap and Overture Maps data.
articles.body_html:
I wanted a picture of the street I grew up on, drawn like an old isometric game. I couldn't find a tool that did it from real map data, so I wrote one.

npx dioramap "Eiffel Tower, Paris" -t night

About ten seconds later there's a poster in the current folder. A place name, a street address or a pair of coordinates all work.

Where the data comes from

  • Nominatim, OpenStreetMap's geocoder, finds the place.
  • Roads, water, parks and land use come from OpenFreeMap vector tiles.
  • Buildings come from Overture Maps, which merges OpenStreetMap with Microsoft and Google footprints. Towns that are thin on OpenStreetMap still get their buildings this way.

The buildings are read straight out of Overture's PMTiles file and the rest from static vector tiles. There's no server of mine in the middle, so there's no API key and no rate limit.

Heights and roofs

Buildings keep their mapped parts, heights and roof shapes. That's how the Eiffel Tower gets its tapering legs and St Peter's gets its dome. When nobody mapped a height, I guess one from the footprint and how built-up the area around it is.

Making it look like pixel art

three.js renders the scene into a render target at a third of the final size, using the 2:1 camera angle pixel artists use. On top of that go outlines, sun shadows, lit windows, trees and cars. Then the image is scaled up with nearest-neighbour filtering, so every edge stays hard.

There's no AI model anywhere in the pipeline. That's why it never comes out blurry.

Video and GIF

--video makes an MP4 where the flat street map rises into the city building by building, then night falls and the lights come on. The headless browser encodes the H.264 frames with WebCodecs and I write the MP4 container myself, so you don't need ffmpeg.

npx dioramap "Dubai Marina" -t night --video
npx dioramap "Rialto Bridge, Venice" --gif

What it can't do

How good it looks depends on the map data. Big cities come out great. A village nobody has mapped in detail looks sparse, and dioramap won't invent buildings to fill it in.

Try it

You need Node 20 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium installed.

npx dioramap "your street, your city"

The code is MIT licensed: https://github.com/omlahore/dioramap

If you render your hometown, I'd like to see it.

articles.title: Building 2D Game Feel in Vanilla JS: Camera Shake, Hitstop, Springs & Object-Pooled Particles
articles.description: A flat Canvas2D square collides with a wall, loses 10 HP, and nothing else happens. No camera kick,...
articles.body_html:
A flat Canvas2D square collides with a wall, loses 10 HP, and nothing else happens. No camera kick, no 45 ms freeze frame, no spring recoil, no sparks. Most HTML5 games feel floaty not because the game loop is broken, but because impact telemetry never reaches the player's eyes and ears.

Instead of pulling in an entire engine just to fix feel, here are four compact vanilla ES Module patterns we extracted from building browser action games—you can test every slider live in our interactive JuiceBox 2D Browser Sandbox before reading a line of theory.

1. Squared Trauma Camera Shake (Per-Frame Decaying Chaos)

Naive random offsets (Math.random() * 10) feel like a jittery UI bug because heavy and light hits decay linearly at identical speed. Using a clamped trauma scalar t in [0, 1] and squaring it (t * t) gives a crisp snap on big strikes and a smooth exponential settle:

export class CameraShake {
  constructor(maxOffset = 18, maxAngle = 0.035, decay = 2.4) {
    this.trauma = 0;
    this.maxOffset = maxOffset;
    this.maxAngle = maxAngle;
    this.decay = decay;
  }

  add(amount) {
    this.trauma = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, this.trauma + amount));
  }

  step(dt) {
    const intensity = this.trauma * this.trauma;
    this.trauma = Math.max(0, this.trauma - this.decay * dt);
    return {
      x: (Math.random() * 2 - 1) * this.maxOffset * intensity,
      y: (Math.random() * 2 - 1) * this.maxOffset * intensity,
      angle: (Math.random() * 2 - 1) * this.maxAngle * intensity,
    };
  }
}

Pairing small rotational tilt (0.02–0.04 rad) with X/Y translation makes explosions feel dramatically heavier than pure X/Y jitter alone.

2. Deterministic Hitstop (Freeze Frames Without Breaking Timers)

A 30–65 ms simulation pause on critical hits lets the brain register collision geometry. The trick is gating simulation updates while keeping particle decay or camera shake slightly responsive—or pausing world dt cleanly with an accumulator:

export class Hitstop {
  constructor() {
    this.remaining = 0;
  }

  trigger(seconds = 0.045) {
    this.remaining = Math.max(this.remaining, seconds);
  }

  consume(dt) {
    if (this.remaining <= 0) return dt;
    this.remaining = Math.max(0, this.remaining - dt);
    return 0; // Pause entity physics during freeze window
  }
}

Inside your requestAnimationFrame loop, pass simDt = hitstop.consume(rawDt) to physics/combat, while camera trauma uses rawDt or decays smoothly once the freeze ends.

3. Critically Damped Spring Physics for Recoil & UI Pop

Hard-coded lerp(a, b, 0.2) depends on frame rate and never overshoots nicely. A damped harmonic spring (stiffness, damping, velocity) produces organic snap on health bars, card hovers, and squash-and-stretch impact scaling:

export class SpringValue {
  constructor(initial = 1, stiffness = 280, damping = 18) {
    this.value = initial;
    this.target = initial;
    this.velocity = 0;
    this.stiffness = stiffness;
    this.damping = damping;
  }

  impulse(kick) {
    this.velocity += kick;
  }

  step(dt) {
    const force = (this.target - this.value) * this.stiffness;
    const accel = force - this.velocity * this.damping;
    this.velocity += accel * dt;
    this.value += this.velocity * dt;
    return this.value;
  }
}

When a character lands from a jump, fire scaleSpring.impulse(-8) and compute scaleX = 1 / scaleY for volume-preserving squash & stretch in two lines.

4. Zero-GC Object-Pooled Particles

Calling particles.push(new Particle()) and filtering arrays every frame triggers GC micro-stutters on mobile browsers. Pre-allocating a fixed typed/object ring and swapping inactive slots keeps frame time flat (0 allocations after boot):

  • Allocate poolSize = 256 slots once at startup.
  • Track activeCount; spawn by overwriting pool[activeCount++].
  • Despawn in O(1) time by swapping the dead particle with pool[--activeCount].

Combined with an additive/alpha fade over life / maxLife, 200 simultaneous sparks cost under 0.2 ms per frame.
